subtopic: APPLICATION OF EXCISE TAX PROVISIONS TO REPLACEMENT TIRES AND TUBES
speechtext:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that last night the general theme of my remarks was an accusation levelled at the opposition, for leaving out of its criticism and discussion of government policy the actual problems and difficulties which must necessarily be considered if a practical legislative measure is to be adopted. I referred to the tactics employed by the opposition and the criticism they had levelled at the government with regard to the 1953 budget. Looking over the speeches of members of the opposition it will be seen that there has been a variety of criticism. Some have claimed that this was a good budget as it was intended to be used as an election budget. To others it was a thoroughly bad budget. But no one considered for a moment that it was an absolutely necessary budget based upon the requirements of the Canadian, people.
In order to recall to the house the different problems that had arisen since the end of the last war, I had referred to the speech which was to be delivered by the late Dr. Clark in December, 1952. Dr. Clark had intended to deal with the situation immediately after the last war and had indicated the aims of this government. He had outlined the methods that would have to be employed if we were going to keep a stable economy.
There were many problems that had to be dealt with at that time by this government. There has been a rapid expansion in our economy and it was necessary to maintain a policy that would maintain the economic equilibrium of our country. One part of that economic policy had to do with taxation, which plays a most important part in the economy of this country. The program that was carried out has had nothing but the loudest praise from leading economists of the world.

It will be recalled that from 1946 to 1949 taxes had been gradually decreased until they were back to what they had been previous to the war. The opposition has claimed that the government reduced taxes in 1949 because it was an election year and then as evidence of bad faith they increased taxes in 1950. The opposition has forgotten to mention that the Korean crisis broke out in 1950 and the opposition were the first to urge a huge national defence program.
There is not one member in this house, either on this or on the opposite side, who cannot see a direct relationship between our huge national defence program and increased taxation. As I say, the Korean war broke out in 1950 and brought with it a series of new problems. It was not the type of war that could be finished in a few years. It has turned out to be a long drawn-out war which may last possibly ten, fifteen or twenty years, and the government's taxation policy must be adapted to those particular circumstances. That was the type of war that had to be waged.
National defence had to be organized and at the same time it was necessary that business should carry on as usual so that free enterprise would not have to reduce its productive capacity. So the government changed its tactics. It was decided that price controls were no longer applicable because the maintenance of such controls over a long period of time would of necessity impair the productive capacity of the country. On the other hand, it would be practically impossible to maintain those price controls over a long period of time from the administrative point of view. Finally, price controls would not have hit at the root causes of the inflation which we all wanted to avoid at that time. Therefore the government did what it could do. It relied on direct methods through its fiscal, monetary and credit policies and supplemented them with a few practical direct controls. In that way it solved the problem facing the country at that time. In 1950 there was an increase in taxes of 20 per cent and no one could possibly expect otherwise in view of the organization of the national defence program. In 1951 there was another effective increase of 10 per cent. In 1952, which I should like to remind the house was not an election year, taxes were reduced by 9 per cent, and in 1953 they were reduced by 11 per cent. We have completed the cycle. Once again we are back to pre-Korea and pre-wartime tax rates. But the government is still carrying on its war effort in Korea and maintaining its forces in Europe. It is still working on its national defence program, and there is still prosperity in Canada.
68108-163i
The Budget-Mr. Cardin
A great part of the opposition's criticism is directed at the reduction in corporate income taxes. There are two excellent reasons why corporate income taxes were reduced. The first was to encourage corporations and industries to continue and to increase, if possible, their productive capacity. There is not one member of this house or one Canadian taxpayer who does not realize that an increase in the productive capacity of industry means that the workman is assured of a job, of higher wages and continued prosperity. The second reason why corporate taxes were reduced was to encourage all Canadian citizens to invest, no matter in how small a measure, in sound Canadian corporations and thereby profit from the extraordinary economic development that is taking place in Canada today. Thus all the benefits to be derived from our natural resources will not be left to foreign capital.
I feel that the criticism of the opposition is entirely unjustifiable because it does not consider the problems or the purposes of the over-all Canadian economic policy. I would invite any member of the house or any person outside of the house to go over the speeches of members of the opposition for the past ten, fifteen or twenty years and try to piece together, if they can, anything that remotely resembles a sound financial policy. I would also invite the Canadian public to consider seriously what would have happened to our economic equilibrium if the government had put into effect the most eloquent but very contradictory suggestions that have been offered by the opposition to the government. The government may not be as oratorical as the Progressive Conservative party, nor is it as sensational as the C.C.F. party, nor as miraculous as the Social Credit party, but it is by far more practical than any of these. It is a sound, serious and logical government that reflects the sincerity, integrity and competence of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who to my mind is the personification of the ideal Canadian.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is one of the pleasantries connected with the House of Commons that an hon. member may, though he disagrees with the material contained in a speech, congratulate a new member upon his maiden effort in the house.
I should like to take the opportunity this afternoon to congratulate the hon. member who has just resumed his seat on having overcome the first hurdle of what I am sure will be a long and distinguished career in the life of Canada. I hope that the occasion will arise before the end of the session when he will be able to make a further contribution. I should like to take the opportunity

The Budget-Mr. Pearkes to congratulate him upon his obvious sincerity and the excellence of his delivery.
Sometimes we are apt to lose sight of the very intimate connection between local problems and decisions which are arrived at by the House of Commons. Therefore I propose to devote some portion of my remarks to affairs connected with my own part of Canada and to endeavour to show how the problems which are facing the far west of this country are intimately related to the decisions made by the federal government. During the past ten years there has been a tremendous growth in the population of the southwestern corner of British Columbia, particularly on Vancouver island where there has been a great influx of people from other parts of Canada and from other countries in the world.
They have taken up residence in the vicinity of Victoria, in the municipalities of Esquimalt and Saanich and up the east coast of the island along the fertile valleys which lie between the central mountain range of the island and the sea dividing Vancouver island from the mainland. As indicative of the numbers that have come, since the last census was taken it has been necessary to divide my own constituency of Nanaimo into two constituencies without adding any appreciable territory to either one. Naturally it is with a somewhat heavy heart that I realize that, no matter what happens when another election is called, my intimate association with at least half of the constituency of Nanaimo will have to be severed.
That is an indication of the large number of people moving into the area and the increase in the population. People moving to Vancouver island have had to be housed, and that has constituted a grave problem in the neighbourhood of Victoria. Although there has been much building activity the amount of serviceable land which is available on which to construct new homes has been extremely limited, with the result that the municipalities have had to develop new areas and to provide those new areas with all necessary municipal servicing such as roads, drainage, sewers, water supplies and so forth. That has placed on the municipal governments a very severe burden.
The burden has been enhanced by the encroachments which are being made continually by federal and provincial governments on what used to be the sphere of municipal taxation. The main problem or the dilemma in which municipal councils find themselves is that of providing the necessary services, maintaining their schools, their roads, their social welfare services, etc., and also keeping the cost of taxation down


within limits so that there is not fear of householders losing their property through oppressive property taxation.
The problem in regard to social services, I think, applies particularly to the municipalities on Vancouver island because, with the moderate climate we enjoy there, a great many elderly people from other parts of Canada move to Vancouver island. Therefore, municipalities are faced with the need of providing more social services than are perhaps provided in other municipalities across Canada.
The problems I am referring to however are not confined purely to Vancouver island. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce at its twenty-third annual meeting, in general session at Toronto in October of last year, had this to say:
Municipalities have been subject to heavy increases in expenditure for both municipal education and welfare services. These increased costs, despite some alleviation by way of grants and other assistance from provincial governments, have borne heavily on the real property tax base. As a result, present and prospective high levels of property taxation are one of the major deterrents to vigorous building programs and the provision of adequate housing and municipal services.
So, this question of providing adequate housing for the residents of Vancouver island is by no means unique. It applies to every municipality which has a growing population, across the whole of Canada. Attention has been drawn to it by the chamber of commerce in their general session. The financial position of these Canadian municipalities is obviously of national concern. It is not merely an immediate local problem. Because of high taxation on much of the property, we find that today even many industries are being forced to relocate their plants.
To find out how federal and provincial governments have been invading or encroaching upon municipalities it is interesting to note that before the war the dominion government took 51 cents out of every tax dollar, thereby leaving 49 cents to be divided between the provincial and municipal authorities. In the most recent figures that I have available the federal government now taxes 77 cents out of the tax dollar, leaving only 23 cents to be divided between the various provincial and municipal authorities. Since pre-war days the Canadian tax bill on all three levels, that is federal, provincial and municipal, has increased from $894 million in 1938 to approximately $6 billion in 1952. In the former year taxes took 18 per cent of the national total production; in the latter 26 per cent. Now, on a per

capita basis the average Canadian in 1938 paid $80 in the year, whereas in 1952 he paid close to $430.
In a report published in the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 15, they attributed this difficulty being placed upon the municipality largely to a vast increase in the spending by the dominion government. The report pointed out that last year, that would be 1952, the municipalities have spent just over twice what they spent in 1938- $600 million as against $273 million.
Making all due allowances for inflation municipalities are spending a fraction more than they did during the war, if you assume that the Canadian dollar, as is frequently stated, is worth about 50 cents today on the basis of what the Canadian dollar was worth before the war. The provinces spent $1 billion in 1952 as against $186 million in 1938. Allowing for a similar rate of inflation their spending has gone up almost three times. But the federal government spending has gone up close to ten times in dollar value and close to five times when allowance is made for dollar deterioration. In 1938 the dominion government spent $436 million. Last year its spending amounted to $4,653 million according to the table given in the recent budget speech. Furthermore, there is no attempt this year to ease the federal tax burden. This budget increases rather than decreases the tax load of the Canadian people.
The forecast of all revenue for the fiscal year 1953-54 indicates a' total budgetary revenue of $4,473 million as compared with $4,374 million collected in the fiscal year 1952-53. With old age security taxes running over $278 million, as compared with $224 million in 1952-53, one notices that there is a general increase in the tax burden of $100 million, which I think is a record for all time, in peace, in respect of the taxation load which the people of Canada are asked to carry. Such reductions in taxation as are being made are being drawn from the anticipated surplus rather than from any cutting down of expenditures.
Now, there are two main causes contributing to the financial plight of the municipalities across this country. The first is undoubtedly the policy followed by the federal government of extracting higher and higher taxation at the federal level; the second that of tax-free federal property within municipal boundaries. In respect of the former policy of requiring municipalities to pay a sales tax on equipment and other articles for municipal purposes, a burden is placed upon municipal bodies from which the provincial governments are relieved.
The Budget-Mr. Pearkes
In his report to the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, held in Calgary last July, Professor D. C. Corbett, director of public administration at McGill university, recommended both the removal of the federal sales tax on goods purchased by municipalities and the exemption from municipal taxation of crown property. I understand that for years the Canadian municipalities have sought, through the medium of the federation of mayors and municipalities, to have supplies and materials, purchased solely for municipal purposes, exempted from the federal 10 per cent sales tax in exactly the same way as the exemption is now granted to provincial governments, their boards, commissions, hospitals and so forth. The municipalities, which are now carrying a financial burden of a remarkable nature, would find some relief at a comparatively small cost to the federal government if the minister could see his way clear to making another correction in the budget by granting this exemption.
There has been widespread disappointment expressed all across the country that no action was taken to exempt municipalities from the sales tax in this year's budget. A few days ago I received the following telegram from the mayor of Victoria:
It is with deep consternation that no provision for exemption of municipal purchases from federal ten per cent sales tax despite earnest effort made by municipal governments. Why should senior levels of government he granted this exemption when local governments avenues of income are being progressively reduced. The continued imposition of the federal sales tax on municipalities is duplicate taxation. Local governments cannot be rated with commerce and industry as our operations are non-profit and have no other recourse but to pass this tax to local taxpayers. Request that government review and extend exemption of federal ten per cent sales tax to municipalities.
I just hope that the minister will find the opportunity, even at this eleventh hour, to reconsider the position with regard to the removal of this exemption from sales tax.
Now, a particularly vicious form of the application of that sales tax was aired at a recent meeting of the Victoria city council's finance committee, when protests were made against the 10 per cent federal sales tax being levied upon articles which the city itself manufactured for its own use. The city controller reported an assessment of $3,928 of arrears, plus $350 by way of penalty and interest that had been made on unpaid sales tax. The items upon which this payment was demanded were such everyday, matter-of-fact things as garbage cans, street signs and mimeographing, which had been made by the city for its own use and not for sale. Street signs, home-made tin cans and mimeographed pieces of paper are surely

The Budget-Mr. Pearkes not articles which have been manufactured within the ordinary meaning of that word. Surely this sales tax was not meant to apply to items which were not manufactured for sale. It was intended, I should think, for articles which were to be sold.
One wonders how a sales tax can be imposed on an article which has not been sold, but which is merely an essential article for city services. It is no wonder that one of the aldermen at this meeting is reported to have referred to the federal government as having neither conscience nor ethics, and that it was motivated solely by a policy of grab, grab, grab. These signs were not made for sale or resale. This was in no way a commercial venture. The only object of the corporation was to save its ratepayers a little money. These signs were not sold; they were not made for sale. They passed through no other hands than through the employees of the city street department, which employees are public servants and paid out of public funds. The garbage cans were made solely for public use. I cannot believe that this parliament ever intended that the sales tax should be applied in such a ruthless manner.
It is almost dictatorship running wild when the central government penalizes a municipal government that is endeavouring to save its taxpayers a little money by making its own road signs, while at the same time the federal government takes unto itself the right to exempt crown property from municipal taxation. I think it is no wonder that the city council rose in anger.
During that discussion, attention was drawn to the fact that the Belmont building, upon which this government pays no taxes to the city, is partially rented by the government. This brings me to Professor Corbett's recommendation and the second of the causes I stated as contributing to the financial plight of municipalities today, namely the tax-free federal property. The payment of municipal taxes on government property, or even an adequate grant in lieu of taxes, would be a means of relieving the burden on municipalities all across Canada. I said a few years ago in this house, and I repeat it now, that the municipality of Esquimalt is a horrible example of the crippling effect on development of a municipality having large areas of federal government tax-free property within its boundaries. Approximately 30 per cent of the total area of Esquimalt is now owned by the federal government. These properties are located, in the main, in three large blocks, namely, the army area having a frontage on Victoria harbour; the navy and dockyard area which

has a frontage on Esquimalt harbour; and the naval area east of Admiral's road. These three areas take up many of the choicest industrial and residential sites in the municipality. Though they are three separate areas, they are all interdependent because they are all connected with the same Department of National Defence. Communications between these three great blocks must be over municipal roads; and the nature of the activities carried out on these various blocks requires the movement of many heavy vehicles passing from one to the other. Yet the federal government contributes little to the maintenance of the roads in that municipality because, under the Municipal Grants Act, a grant is payable only to what is referred to as class A federal property for which material services are provided.
The provision and maintenance of public roads and sidewalks are specifically excluded in the act from the term "service". The roads which were constructed by this municipality were never in the first instance designed for the heavy vehicles which are now used by the Department of National Defence. The roads and streets are visibly deteriorating as a result of the extensive and continually increasing use by these vehicles.
There is a great deal of construction work now going on at H.M.C.S. Naden. New barracks are being constructed and these heavy vehicles are plowing up and down the roads immediately opposite, making them practically impassable for the residents in the area. Such grants as this municipality of Esquimalt has received in the past-and last year they amounted to in the neighbourhood of $25,000 to cover almost 500 acres of tax-free property within the municipal boundaries-are totally inadequate to maintain the services which the municipality is called upon to provide. On account of the fact that much of this property is waterfront property-and if this property were privately owned it would have been developed for high-class residential areas or for industrial areas because of the vicinity of water transport and also of the railway which runs close to that area-fair value to be placed on this government property would be approximately $2,500 an acre. Shipyard property adjacent to the dockyard property has been assessed at a value of $3,000 an acre.
Hence if the grant were based even on the assessed value of the federal property, without any consideration being given to such improvements as have been constructed on the property-and if it was in private use, of course, the improvements would have been taken into consideration-the municipality

would receive much fairer treatment. The present year's mill rate is 52. If that rate was applied to federal property on a valuation of $2,500 per acre, then again a more reasonable formula would have been arrived at for calculating the basis of the grant.
Another feature which is unique so far as Esquimalt is concerned is the fact that it is in close proximity to the city of Victoria, with the result that the commercial concerns in Victoria supply the needs of those who are employed on the federal and service properties. It is for these reasons-and others which I could mention if there were sufficient time in which to do so-that I feel that Esquimau is entitled to special consideration which would result in a far more substantial grant being allocated to that municipahty than is being made at the present time.
Esquimau, however, is only an outstanding example-and perhaps a pronounced one-of the intolerable burden which is being placed on all small municipalities owing to the extent of government-owned, non-taxable property within their boundaries. The position of Esquimalt may be unique in some respects. I do not believe it could be duplicated anywhere else across Canada. Other municipalities, however, are affected and suffer in varying degrees. There is much government-owned property, for instance, in Victoria and some in the adjacent municipality of Saanich. It would therefore seem that if much-needed assistance is to be brought to all municipalities in order to enable them to meet their obligations, the principle of tax-free property needs a thorough review in order that a practice workable a century ago may be adapted to modern conditions.
Another problem I just referred to, which is closely associated with Vancouver island and for which no provision has been made in this budget, is the problem of the pensioner and the veteran. We have heard it stated by hon. members on this side of the house that little has been done for the little man. There is no indication whatever of any consideration being given to the possibility of increasing the war veterans allowance, for instance, which is the only income that many old soldiers have. I believe the municipalities could have had relief shown to them and I believe that the pensioners and the ex-soldiers

the little man-could also have been looked after if a firm effort had been made to eliminate waste, extravagance and inefficiency to which reference has been made.
A few years ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) made the proud boast that there
The Budget-Mr. Pearkes was no waste, duplication or extravagance in any of the departments. I believe that he was perfectly sincere when he made that boast. I am pleased that his sense of decency has made him refrain from repeating it this year, because the reports of the Auditor General, reports of the public accounts committee, the Currie report and so forth have shown quite obviously that there has been waste and extravagance. I am afraid that the same spirit still exists and is shown in this budget because, as I have already said, the reductions which are to take place appear to come from the surplus rather than from cutting out expenditures.
The Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production have come under a good deal of criticism in connection with this budget and other matters which have been before the house. It seems to me that the main criticism can be directed against the non-defence expenditures in both the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production. I did claim not very long ago that the Department of Defence Production might well be called the department of defence construction. It seems to me that advantage is being taken of the sympathetic attitude of the Canadian people towards national security by allowing the defence departments to develop permanent improvements which will be of advantage, perhaps, to the services at some future date, rather than an immediate contribution to the defence of this country or to the obligations we have to meet in the international field.
Recently attention was called to the fact that we are spending millions on the construction of permanent camps, also on the establishment of defence communities in which large numbers of residences have been built. I do suggest that they have been built without due consideration for economy. The various houses themselves are widely separated, requiring very extensive landscaping programs. And we have been acquiring a great deal of land.
I need only refer to the question of the new training area which has been purchased in New Brunswick, and which may run up to $35 million or more. And already there are training areas in that province and in other parts of Canada. Then, there is the construction of many permanent buildings. These are mostly being built on the cost-plus basis, which everyone admits is about as extravagant a way of building as it is possible to have.
All these examples, and very many others, can be found in the report of the public accounts. But there are other expenditures

The Budget-Mr. Pearkes about which it is impossible to obtain any information. And if we ask questions about some of these other expenditures we are told that this is breaking security. I asked questions the other day regarding an operation referred to as Pine Tree, which I did not know very much about. I wanted to get some information. Obviously it has to do with the provision of electronics and that sort of thing in the northern part of our country. My question was not an idle one; it did not arise from my brain, but was based on letters I had received from irate taxpayers who were complaining about waste and extravagance. Whether their complaints were made justly or not I cannot tell, until I have made inquiries.
I think the government should recognize the fact that when questions are asked in the house or put on the order paper they have been prompted by taxpayers who want to know the answers. It is rather disconcerting when, having tried to find out certain information about the provision of electronics and being told that this is a security matter and must not be asked, one finds that a circular letter has been sent around shortly before, of which some 110,000 copies have been issued to people in and out of the services, and in which the gentleman who just resigned as chief of the air staff said that some $150 million had been spent on electronics, and that this did not include those electronics intimately implicated with armament projects. Obviously the total must run into hundreds of millions.
These questions which I and other members have asked are, as I said before, based on reports and letters we have received. And I have received ugly stories which have been coming out from the north. Because of the degree of security that is necessary I cannot and will not mention the locations of the projects to which I now refer. But my information has come from reliable sources. I have seen some of the people; and those I have not been able to see, myself, I have had my solicitor call upon.
These are just a few quotations which, I suggest, will bear out the justification of the inquiries we have been making. One taxpayer writes to me that the-
-over-all opinion of the administration of his portion of the job was that there was a flagrant disregard of cost.
And another:
In one instance, particularly, material was shipped and followed very shortly afterwards by an identical shipment which had not been requested, and which was useless to them. This obviously is just plain bad management.
And another:
$14,000 worth of tools and parts, ordered and shipped; of these only one carton arrived and when 

opened it contained two wrenches and a large amount of useless scrap metal. The rest of the shipment, though dispatched, has never arrived.
And then again:
Actual technical equipment installed on the job was purchased at a price four or five times in excess of the normal cost thereof.

speechtext: Order. There is a question as to whether or not the hon. member should quote letters, especially when he is making charges, without giving the names of the persons who have written the letters. The rule is that he must be prepared to give the names.

speechtext: On the point of order; this matter has been discussed a number of times. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The rule is that if a minister quotes an official document he must table the document, but not a private communication. If the hon. member wishes to make these charges upon his own responsibility then that is a different matter. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Some people have not been able to see me personally because they are not in this immediate vicinity.
