I do feel that there should be an examination into these expenditures. Had a real and earnest effort been made to cut down this waste and extravagance, I believe the Minister of Finance would have found his task much easier and have been able to give relief to the municipalities to which I referred in the earlier part of my address and to those groups of citizens who find the burden of the present cost of living most excessive.
* Mr. J. J. Smith (Moose Mountain): Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I do not intend to deal in great detail with the budget itself, as it seems to me that practically everything that can be said has been said and I do not care to make a speech of repetition. I do not intend to bring the problems of my constituency before the house, as the hon. member who has just spoken has done. I have another way of doing that. There are plenty of problems in my constituency. When I am told of a problem I go to the minister who has to do with that matter and I have been fairly successful in recent years. It may have been imagination, but when I came here first I felt that some of the minister's offices were a little hard to get into. I felt that I was getting more excuses than reasons. But that has been all cleared up, and now I am told why a thing is done when I go to a minister. That is all I ask. As I say, I have been fairly successful. When I am not successful I realize that it is either because I have a poor case or because I have presented it badly.
There is one problem that has arisen in my constituency which has to do with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). I refer to the method of making income tax collections as practised by a few of the officials of that department who have been operating in my province and in my constituency.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you fixed that with the minister?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not been able to yet. I have been asked that question and so far I cannot answer it. I
2568	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith never leave at the end of a session to go back to my constituency without being able to answer practically all the questions that I assume might be asked as to why the government does this or does that.
I have been asked why a few jokers-I underline the few-in the collection department should think that because they have a brief-case and a government job they can push everyone around. You might almost think that they owned the country. I shall come back to that later. Before I go on I do want to say that we are most fortunate in having a Minister of National Revenue who treats all people alike. It is just too bad when we have such an efficient department with so many officials doing a good job that a few should be spoiling the whole thing. I shall come back to this point later.
I said that I was not going to deal with the budget at any great length, but I do want to refer to the speech made by the leader of the C.C.F. party. I realize immediately that in trying to deal with the speech delivered by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) he has it all over me in being a most able speaker with long experience and, in addition, a good artist.
I heard the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar make that speech twenty years ago in Saskatchewan, or one just like it. I would not suggest that he is not sincere in his remarks, because after anyone tells a story for twenty years he is bound to believe it himself. I am not going to suggest that he should not continue telling it because he has had such good results in Saskatchewan from telling that same story.
I am not going to suggest that he should not use it in the next federal election. Corporations are something that we know very little about in Saskatchewan. I give the hon. member full credit for being a great artist in drawing the picture he did. There is only one greater artist that I know of, the premier of Saskatchewan. He is much better. I can just picture those two hon. gentlemen going around Saskatchewan during the next campaign making practically the same speech that was made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It would possibly be unparliamentary if I said that they will be telling just half the truth, but anyway they will be giving just half the facts and telling only part of the story.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, coming to this house and knowing little about finance, and I admit at once knowing little about corporations, 1 found myself in quite an awkward position in dealing with the situation. I am sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) or his parliamentary assistant, yes,
[Mr. Smith (Moose Mountain) .1

even the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), could have done it much better. However, when the campaign starts we in the province of Saskatchewan-I have said this before and I repeat it whether or not hon. members agree with me-have what is in my opinion the most effective political, and I underline the word "political," opposition to the government. Possibly that should be a compliment to the members of the opposition from our province. When the campaign gets under way, however, we pretty well have to deal with the situation ourselves. If the Minister of Finance were in my constituency and had explained to the people just what corporations are, then I would not have to do it. I do not expect he will be there so therefore I am going to attempt to put the whole story on Hansard.
I hold no brief for any corporation whatsoever. I might mention in passing that I have a brother in the city of Winnipeg who was at one time a farmer. He went to the city of Winnipeg and is now in a partnership business. He tells me he is paying double taxation. Each time I pass through Winnipeg, both coming and going, he complains that it is an unjust tax. As a matter of fact I have another brother in the province of Saskatchewan who thinks that corporations should be soaked more heavily. I tell this to the Minister of Finance in order to show him that it is not possible to please everybody. I do not think it would make any difference what tax cuts were made. My C.C.F. brother in Saskatchewan would still not be in favour of the budget. That brother is well known to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He knows him personally, and so far as their views on corporations are concerned they are as much alike as two peas. I mention that in passing to indicate to the Minister of Finance that so far as my family is concerned he could not produce a budget which would please us all. One is a socialist, another was a Conservative in the last election, and I stand in the middle.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar tried to picture the budget as a rich man's budget. I repeat that I hold no brief for corporations. If it is a rich man's budget, if I thought for a moment that the present government is legislating for the rich man, then I would have to say that I am in the wrong camp.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are more welcome over here anyway.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should join your brother in Winnipeg.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Naturally I was somewhat concerned whether it was a

rich man's budget so I conducted some research. I may say I have no ghost writers. I do not speak with notes although my speech would possibly read much better if I did. But that does not make a great deal of difference because I do not send my speeches to my constituents. I do not suppose anyone else reads them so it does not make any difference how they read. In any event, I was quite concerned. As a matter of fact, as I said, I heard the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar make the same speech 20 years ago at a place 20 miles from our farm. Although at that time he told us what the socialists would do if they were in power, he neglected to do so in his speech on the budget. At that time he convinced me. Of course I was good bait in the thirties. I remember well that on that day in 1932 when we went to hear the hon. gentleman we had been threshing a crop of wheat on our farm. It was my father's farm and my two brothers and I were still at home. We had 12,000 bushels of wheat. That was in the drought year of 1932 and we sold the first part of it for 32 cents a bushel and the balance for 19 cents. Naturally I was fairly good bait for that kind of speech.
That was before I had the right to exercise my franchise and I suppose I am not so flexible now, but at the same time the hon. member almost convinced me the other day that the Minister of Finance had produced a rich man's budget. I examined the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar after listening to his address in the house. I do not want to take anything from it. I could quote what he said but I will not do that. What he did say dealt with corporations. In my opinion he tried to paint a picture of corporations and large companies as being a group of millionaires. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar took an income tax form, put in some imaginary figures and worked out the answer. I presume that his figures were correct.
But when he was putting that picture before the house the Minister of Finance suggested that corporations had already paid 49 per cent or 50 per cent on the dividends that were paid to their shareholders. The leader of the C.C.F. did not want to hear that at all. He could not go along with that kind of argument. Perhaps I might quote a short passage from the discussion that took place. At page 2351 of Hansard for February 24 there is the following:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is paid at the rate of 50 per cent as the result of his interest in the companies.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a minute. Is the hon. gentleman going to argue that he has paid something? He has paid nothing, and so far as the companies in which he is interested are concerned they pass on any tax assessed against them to the general
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith public. The general public pays that tax which this gentleman escapes in his personal income tax. I think that is a fairly complete answer to the minister's suggestion.
If, that is the case, if the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar wants it that way, then while I am not an expert on finance and I do not know whether or not that is correct we will go along with him for a little while. I have a question to ask the C.C.F. party, whose leader spoke for them, I suppose. If it is the case that corporations pass on the taxes to the general public, then why does the C.C.F. ask the Minister of Finance to maintain, or even to raise, the taxes on corporations when the C.C.F. party says that those taxes are passed on to the general public? For whom are they speaking? Are they speaking for the general public? Of course we know they are not interested in corporations-at least they claim they are not. Possibly the C.C.F. member who is going to follow me shortly will give the house and myself the benefit of an answer to my question as to why they suggest that the Minister of Finance should maintain a high corporation tax that is passed on to the general public.
I went to the trouble of hunting up a few facts and figures on corporations. I choose first the Massey-Harris Company. I do not have the companies the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar used. They are in eastern Canada and we in western Canada know nothing about them. I have taken companies that will be a little closer to his door, indeed, in the constituency he represents. There are the Massey-Harris dealers. I might ask, possibly for the third time, why the hon. member asks the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to maintain a corporation tax on the Massey-Harris Company when he himself says that the Massey-Harris people and other corporations will pass the taxes on to the consumer. I think in the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar farmers buy about as much machinery as they do in any other constituency. Possibly we could have an explanation of it all from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), as he is a farmer and understands all aspects of farming, and he is an eloquent speaker with much more experience than I have. Possibly he could give us an answer. If he does not see fit to give an answer to the house, as we have almost daily conversations, although sometimes we see who can tell the other the biggest lie, possibly he will give me a reason for his leader making such a statement.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what about the Massey-Harris Company? They have 16,717 shareholders. I do not suppose they are all millionaires, and when we track down the
2570	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith dividends it would not appear that way. According to the company's annual report for 1952 the Minister of Finance got $12,550,000 from Massey-Harris. The dividends to the 16,717 shareholders, according to this report, were $4,617,205. My arithmetic is not too good but it is better than my spelling, and if you divide that total dividend by the number of shareholders, by simple arithmetic it gives each shareholder $276.10. The C.C.F. would not say that would indicate that the shareholders were millionaires nor that they should not have that dividend. There is another surprising figure here. The number of shareholders is, as I say, 16,717, while the number of employees-world wide-is 18,930. They have almost as many shareholders as they have people working for the company throughout the world.
Those were interesting figures to me and I thought possibly it might be well if I gave them to the house, and more particularly to my colleagues from the province of Saskatchewan. We will have to fight the battle out there and, if they have not done any homework on the budget address, they can take what I have given and go on from there.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did Massey-Harris pay in patronage dividends?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Maybe you can find it here in this annual report. I will send it over to you in a few minutes and you can look at it when I am through.
I think possibly I will now go on to another company, the Bell Telephone Company. That company is pretty close to us in Saskatchewan although I do not suppose there are a lot of shareholders out there. Strangely enough, the other day in the coffee shop I heard a conversation when my hon. friend from Swift Current (Mr. Whiteside) was sitting with me. I am going to tell this story just to show the house how vulnerable the people of Saskatchewan are to this kind of C.C.F., socialistic propaganda talk.
We had been seated at the table and were having coffee. There was a gentleman with us whose name I do not know, and there were two ladies at the next table. They were talking about shares in a company. One young and rather attractive lady started talking about her shares in this company and asked the gentleman at our table whether he thought she should sell her shares or not. I immediately thought to myself: Well, if I were single and fifteen years younger there would be a rich young lady for me. Of course, Mr. Speaker, I am married and I did not entertain that idea long. I am happily married too-and I say that because it is a


fact and I am not too sure but what my wife might be in the gallery.
Anyway, I listened to the conversation about shares. The gentleman said he did not like to advise the lady as to whether she should sell her shares but he suggested that she might sell half of them. I thought that this young lady must be quite rich. Finally the gentleman asked her how many shares she had. She gave a cute little smile, blushed and said she had $160 worth. Now, that just goes to show you that not only the rich have company shares.
Anyway, I happened to hear her say that the shares were in the Bell Telephone Company. This morning, at a quarter after four and from then on, I was thinking about the speech I was going to make, and I remembered the young lady speaking about her shares and I decided I would find out something about the Bell Telephone Company and who owned its shares. This morning I telephoned the company and a lady answered. I told her exactly what I wanted, and that, being a dumb individual from Saskatchewan, I did not know too much about the corporation. She was glad to give me what I needed. I first asked her how many shareholders there were in the Bell Telephone Company. She said that roughly there were 100,000 shareholders. I asked if many of the employees bought shares in the company and she said yes, that she put all her savings in the Bell Telephone Company. She said she did not own anything except her clothes and her shares in the company. She said they had a very nice system of payroll deductions which made it convenient for employees of the company to invest in its shares.
I began to ask her more questions and at that point she put me in touch with someone who could give me all the information. I then spoke to a Mr. Dockstader, assistant to the president of the company, and told him exactly what I wanted. He was very glad to help and he provided me with this report for which I sent a messenger. The matter gets closer to Saskatchewan because I notice that Mr. C. A. Dunning, P.C., of Montreal, happens to be one of the directors. This report which I have here indicates that there are 100,890 shareholders and the dividends are a little in excess of $22,570,000. The Minister of Finance received a little more than $23 million from the Bell Telephone Company.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a big shareholder.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, he is a big shareholder. However, this is a company on which the C.C.F. thinks the Minister of Finance should pile more corporation

taxes. These figures, and what I have mentioned, indicate that there are a lot of people in the Bell Telephone Company and it does not look a bit as if there are only a few millionaires. I do not think the C.C.F. should suggest that the 100,000 shareholders of the Bell Telephone Company are a select group of millionaires.
Now I am going to deal with the Canadian Pacific Railway and that company gets still closer to home. I hope the leader of the C.C.F. has no objection to my taking companies so close to home. I did not have a report on the Canadian Pacific, other than a report on the number of shareholders. I had to telephone to Montreal to get this. The number of shareholders in the Canadian Pacific totals 63,751. I have not been able to get in touch with anyone in Ottawa who has shares in the Canadian Pacific, but I happen to know two individuals close to where 1 live. Both of them are widows at the moment. One is related to me by marriage, and her husband died two years ago the day after New Year's. As a matter of fact, I had New Year's supper with him. The next morning his "ticker" quit, and he went out like a light. This woman had her husband's life savings invested in shares in the Canadian Pacific.
I do not know just how many shares she had. I know of another individual, who is also a widow in my constituency, and whose husband died a few years ago. I know a little about this case because I happened to be an executor of the estate. Anyone who has had anything to do with estates would know about this. There were three executors, and I was appointed to cash the cheques which she received from the Canadian Pacific. I do know her financial position. She is the wife of a former section foreman who died shortly before he was to be superannuated. I know that she was left with one crippled child, and all she had when he died was the furniture in that section house and $10,000 in Canadian Pacific shares. I do not think the leader of the C.C.F. group would suggest that women in this category should have any further taxation imposed upon them. I do not think he would deprive them of these dividends. That is all I am going to say about that.
At the beginning of my speech, Mr. Speaker, I said that I knew I was taking on a pretty big job in attempting to answer a man like the member for Rosetown-Biggar. He is a former school teacher, and has always earned his living by talking. I have only earned part of my living during the last four years by talking, so naturally I am not as experienced as he is.
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith
I see the Minister of National Revenue is now in the house, so I am going to go back and refer, in as kindly a way as I can, to the tax collectors in his department. I believe the minister was in the house when I said that it was too bad, when we had such a fine minister and such an efficient group of officials doing a job which is not a nice job, that we had to have a few "jokers", as I called them, who spoil everything. These people, when given a government brief-case, go out into the country and do a great deal of damage. There have been a few of them in my constituency, and they can make more socialists in a month than I could make Liberals during three months of hard driving. I am now referring to the political aspect of the question.
I do say what I think we need is better public relations in the income tax department. Possibly there are many places where the department has good public relations, but in other places they have not. I do not see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in his seat, but I can tell him that all is not well in his province, either.
I believe I will cite two cases. I do not like to get up and make general statements without citing specific instances. I know that this is not government policy, and I am not quarrelling with government policy in any way, shape or form. I can debate that even with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on any platform, but some of these individuals to whom I refer are not carrying out government policy. When I first came to Ottawa one of the first problems I had -I have had lots of them since-was in connection with an income tax case. The Minister of National Revenue never heard about it. He happened to be in Newfoundland at the time, but we got it fixed up. I did not know the minister at the time I was trying to get in touch with him. This case concerns another widow. It seems to me I hear of the troubles of a lot of widows.
This particular widow was to be fined $10 for not filling out a succession duty form. The income tax division in Regina, I suppose it was, wanted this $10 fine. A friend of mine wrote to me about it. By the way, I knew this lady very well. She was not a supporter of mine, but was a C.C.F.'er. However, that makes no difference to me. When I am in Ottawa I work just as hard as I can for anyone in my constituency, and I do not care what their politics is-except on election day. This lady was to be fined $10 because she had not filled out this succession duty form. Her husband had been receiving old age pension under the means test, so when I could not get in touch with the Minister of National Revenue or his
2572	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith deputy I went over to Sussex street to that building in which the wartime prices and trade board was housed. When I got in there I got lost. I do not recall the name of the person to whom I was speaking, but in any event I asked him to check on this matter. I said that I knew it was the law, but surely you are not going to fine this woman $10. She did not know when you sent this form she had to fill it in. She did fill it in later, but it was too late. The chap to whom I was speaking said he could not do anything about it without the minister. I said that I was sure the minister had not told anyone in the department to just give her so long to pay the $10 or she was going to be brought before a court. This chap assured me that something would be done.
I went home in December, but before that I wrote to my friend and told him that it was fixed up. When I went home my friend told me that this lady was going to be brought before a police magistrate on Saturday and fined if she did not have the amount paid by the Monday. I immediately telephoned to Regina and asked to speak to some official. I think perhaps the first fellow with whom I was speaking was one of those "jokers" I mentioned. I told him that I did not think they had to get $10 from this woman to balance the budget. I said, "If you have to get $10 to balance the budget, you will get a personal cheque from the member for Moose Mountain1 to settle it, but you will not get anything from this woman". I asked to speak to another gentleman, and I told him about it. He said that if that was the case I did not need to send the $10, and he would review the case. I told him I would send it and he could do what he liked with it. I would say that was an example of fairly good public relations, although rather slow.
I wish the Minister of Justice were in his seat, because things are not too good in his province either. I know of a neighbour of mine who went to live in Winnipeg in 1946. He was a fairly successful farmer, and he moved to Winnipeg. He did not fill in an income tax form in Saskatchewan, and I hold no brief for him for not doing so. He claimed that he did not know he had to do so. A brother of mine who lives in Winnipeg told him that I was going through, and to see me. He was having trouble down at the revenue building at the comer of Portage and Main. I went up to the revenue department with him, marched in, and did I get in touch with a "dilly" of a lad. I think his name was McBride. He had been dealing with this neighbour of mine.
I told my friend before we went in that I was not going to mention that I was a
[Mr. Smith (Moose Mountain).!

member of parliament. I do not like people to know that I am a member of parliament when I am away from home. I told him that I would go with him as the reeve of the municipality from which he had come, and try to have the thing straightened out. They got us into a little room and we sat around a table. It was not long until this fellow had the old farmer sweating blood. He was really pouring the questions at him, and I was getting a little warmer all the time. He wanted to know a lot of things, and was in my opinion insulting. Finally, I said to the lad with whom I went, "You gather up your papers and let us get out of here."
This little joker looked at me-I remember him well-and he said: "Who in h- do you think you are?" I said, "That makes no difference. This man is not under arrest. I brought him in here and he is going out with me." I said, "You are making a lot of bother for this man for nothing", and I told him, "I will tell you who I happen to be. I am a member of parliament, although that makes no difference." I said, "You are putting that man to a lot of trouble for nothing. I know he should have been paying his income tax. He is willing to pay it. But you are trying to send him out into Saskatchewan and you are asking him a lot of questions that it is hard for him to get answers for; and anyway, you have them right here. Why don't you assess him? You won't take his answers when and if he can get them." He looked up at me and said, "These farmers are all good poker players. Why should I pull my tricks out of my pocket?"
I do not know of any time in my life that I wanted so badly to slap a man in the mouth and did not do it. I said, "All right. That finishes it. I will go to Ottawa and see the minister, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann)." I went back down to my brother's office. He said, "Oh, no. You don't have to do that." He told me to phone somebody, and he told me whom in the department to telephone. He said, "There are plenty in there who do not think they know everything. Most of them are pretty good." I telephoned the man and told him what I wanted. I said, "I don't want this man to have this trouble and pushing around." I said that he was a good honest chap and that I just wanted him to be treated like any other good Canadian. I said, "I am quite satisfied you will get your money." That was done. The Minister of National Revenue never heard about that case because it was all fixed up. Again I say it is fairly good public relations, but again a little bit clumsy.

Possibly I should say a little bit more about this matter. I had a letter; and talking about letters, I hope the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will not think I am exaggerating. I am only trying to put the facts before him as they are. I have a letter from one who I think is as good a citizen as there is in the Dominion of Canada-yes, and if you like, as good a Liberal as there is, and that takes in a lot of ground. He said to me in the letter: "Smitty, in your constituency the Currie report will cut no ice in the next election." He said, "The South Saskatchewan dam will cut some ice if we don't get it. But none of them has anything to do with what you are going to have to face in what comes in from a few hounds that come into this constituency when you are down there, and are just running after everybody."
I find that what the C.C.F. organizer in the constituency is doing is this. I may be asked by somebody if I can prove it and if I have to, I can; they are running a very technical set-up out there. They send in letters to the income tax department that so and so has not paid his income tax, and if so, not enough. Then what happens? A hound comes out. Maybe he is a socialist, and I would not be surprised if this is the case. The minister's officials are possibly appointed-well, in fact I am quite sure that their appointments are made by the civil service, and you get all kinds of people. But if you get a C.C.F. organizer working with a few income tax collectors who are C.C.F.'ers, you can make it pretty rough. I want to say that we have had a great many income tax collectors in our constituency and they were very good fellows. They would come in and assist the farmers, help the farmers out, and they did a good job.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Send them down to Quebec, Smitty!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member asked me that question. His roommate tried to rub more salt into the wounds a short time ago by raising a smokescreen in this house and trying to suggest that the Minister of National Revenue was playing politics, not having as many tax collectors and not collecting as much in taxes in Ontario and in Quebec as they were in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He had no hounds there.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister replied and made a good job of it. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) got fairly good publicity in many western papers for that speech, but the Minister of National
The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith Revenue, in his reply to it, got just as good publicity. Otherwise he only added salt to the wound by the speech.
We in western Canada do not know too much about corporations. I admit that. But many of the people in western Canada-in my constituency, anyway-came from Ontario and Quebec, or the great percentage of them, and they know perfectly well why the western farmer-that is the large wheat farmer- would be paying more income tax than would the eastern small farmer. For instance, I understand that in the province of Ontario the average farm is 65 acres. I should like to know how many farmers in the province of Saskatchewan or in Manitoba either are paying income tax on a 65-acre farm. There is no such thing at all. It is more socialist propaganda.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You do not pay your income tax on your acreage. It is on your net income.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I might add that I have here an affidavit about -I suppose I could tell about it or I could read it-a sheriff. It is really rough, I want to tell the minister. Of course he does not appoint sheriffs. The sheriff in Estevan is Mr. Cuming. He is known to my C.C.F. friends. He was a casualty of the provincial government and he was appointed sheriff. He is no more qualified to be sheriff than I am qualified to be queen of England. He is there because he was defeated in the election. I do not know whether the minister can do anything about it or not.
What happened was this. I have here a copy of an affidavit. I am not going to mention the name. It is to the effect that an individual was pulled up for income tax. He had a writ of execution against him, and that served him right because he should have been paying his income tax. I do not hold any brief for any man who does not pay his income tax. I think everybody should pay income tax. If they did so, possibly I would pay a little bit less. Anyway, he had a writ of execution against him and a letter from this sheriff to come to the courthouse. He gave particulars on the affidavit, that he went down and after he had paid the sheriff, Mr. Cuming, $500, the sheriff said to him, "That is what you get for voting Liberal."
The gentleman who went in was told that by the sheriff. I have the signed affidavit here that it is a fact. It is not just a letter without a name; it is an affidavit. That is the kind of thing that is going on. I think surely something should be done about it. What drives the farmer against democracy is that kind of thing, in my opinion. That is why the

The Budget-Mr. J. J. Smith people in Russia jumped out of the frying pan into the fire. I would hope that there will be something done to rectify this situation.
I suppose my time is about gone. I am getting to be quite a politician. I used to have a hard time to speak for ten or fifteen minutes. Now I can go on forever, seemingly. In any event, I think possibly I should not sit down before I refer at least a little bit to things having to do with farm problems, although again there is not much need for my talking farm problems on the floor of this house. As I say, I do not send my speeches out to my constituents, and I do not suppose anybody reads them anyway.
I have the privilege of attending the provincial caucus with the minister about once a week. I was in conversation with him yesterday about farm problems. I see the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) practically every day. I do not speak to him every day but do so at least once a week. We are quite concerned about farm problems. Therefore anything I say here today would not add anything to what I do for my constituency. I can do that without making a speech on the floor of the house. But I have here an editorial. It comes from the Estevan Mercury, and it is one with which I wholly agree. I do not as a rule read editorials but I think that possibly this is one that I should read. I am not going to read it all but it is headed "Out of the Market" and reads in part as follows:
The Mercury has in the past often pointed out that we in Canada have been gradually pricing ourselves out of foreign markets because of rising costs with no effort being made to "hold the line".
There has been altogether too much following of the lead set by the United States in all matters creating inflationary conditions which have brought about high costs of labour, raw materials, services and administration.
Farther down it goes on to say as follows:
The inevitable results are beginning to come home to roost. Canadian farm products are produced at high cost-so high that the foreign export market is not going to buy them until other sources are drained.
It goes on here:
For example Britain is buying Argentina dressed beef at 16-6 cents, the Canadian price in Montreal last year was 44 cents. Denmark is supplying bacon at 31-5 cents per pound; Canadian price 42 cents. New Zealand butter is sold to Britain for 36-7 cents; Canadian price 58-8 cents.
We hear it said in the house that the government is responsible for losing the British market. This is all nonsense. I am no more in favour of subsidizing the farmer than I am of protecting industry by tariffs. Therefore let me say that I am not in favour of either of those procedures. I read the comments because I am interested in what

they say, and because I believe they spell out the situation.
The editorial goes on in this way:
Only on wheat has Canada been able to hold its own and that position has been held solely because of quality and an assured supply.
Even the wheat market is altering its complexion. There is yet no certainty that the international wheat agreement will be carried on. National buying of wheat has been discontinued in Britain bringing the individual dealer back into the picture. This just about means the end to international government deals and barter and leaves the individual grain buyer to purchase where he can get the best deal. No one as yet knows what effect this is going to have on the Canadian grain board handling of wheat.
I think it would not toe wise at this time to talk about the international wheat agreement in detail. Then the editorial goes on:
It is unfortunate that the farmer is the one that will get the first knock in this readjustment process, particularly as he was not responsible in any way for the kite-flying. While generally speaking the western farmer has had a few quite prosperous years, these cannot be expected to continue because of high production of wheat particularly and any marked falling in prices that he receives can quite easily wipe out his margin of profit.
The question then arises in his mind as to whether or not he can expect any assistance towards reducing his costs to the point of once again being able to compete on world markets.
That is the question he wants to put to the industrial areas where in a good many cases high wages and short working hours have raised prices on machinery and other things he has to buy thereby increasing his production costs to the point that has priced him out of the world markets.
Well, that is the question, and it is a good question. I am not too greatly worried about what is in store for us. We will work something out, but I cannot see any honeymoon for western agriculture.
That is all I wish to say at this time. I am sorry I have taken up so much time of the house in dealing with corporations about which I knew very little until ten days ago. But I would hope that, for a fellow who knew nothing about corporations, I did not make too bad a job of it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the speech immediately preceding mine, with its breezy reminiscences, mixed up with stories about the hon. member's family, C.C.F. widows, and the like. There was one thing his speech did prove, and that is' that the old adage that people habitually vote as their fathers voted before them is wrong. That was proved by the record of his family. He tells us that in it there are people holding three different political opinions.
Then it was refreshing to hear a Saskatchewan farmer take up the cudgels on behalf of the machine companies.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is mere propaganda. Peddle that somewhere else.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not wish to argue the point. I would have pointed out, however, that instead of referring to the Bell Telephone Company enjoyed-perhaps I should not say enjoyed; perhaps I should say suffered-by the people of Ontario, we have a telephone company in Saskatchewan that has a great many shareholders. It has 750,000 shareholders; it is the Saskatchewan government telephone system, and provides the cheapest service in Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You did not build it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not attempting to reply to my hon. friend's speech. I noticed that he made reference to the arguments offered by my leader. I shall not attempt to defend my leader because, as the hon. member for Moose Mountain has pointed out, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is quite able to defend himself.
Before turning to my particular criticism of the budget, I should like to discuss a matter which has already been brought to the attention of the government by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). I refer to a matter of taxation. The mayor of my city has wired to me and, I believe, to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) as well as to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), pointing out that municipalities, as such, should not be asked to pay the sales tax in respect of equipment they purchase which, under no circumstances, is resold. They suggest that Canadian municipalities should be exempted from this measure of application of the sales tax. I understand that on several occasions the Canadian federation of mayors has endorsed this idea, passed resolutions in regard to it, and forwarded them to the government, but that up to the present time there have been no results.
In the wire I received from the mayor of Saskatoon the municipalities are described as creatures of the provincial government, and it is stated that the provincial governments do not pay the sales tax in this matter. Our city council thinks that cities and other municipalities should not pay such taxes. Surely there is a strong argument for its removal or revocation, particularly in respect of equipment the cities manufacture for themselves, for their own use.
In reference to Saskatoon particularly, there is the matter of prefabricated sidewalk curbs, which are manufactured by the city itself, and upon which it has to pay sales tax. I take this opportunity to bring the
The Budget-Mr. Knight matter to the attention of the house. I have here an editorial from the Star-Phoenix of February 26 which states:
The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities has repeatedly urged the federal government to extend the exemption-
That is to say, the exemption from the sales tax.
-to the municipalities. The request is eminently reasonable. It strikes us as unfair to the municipalities that they should tax their residents in order to pay a tax to the federal government. The municipal tax base is restricted in all parts of Canada. Their taxes fall upon a limited section of the community. Yet the sales tax provision requires them to help support a government that has many sources of revenue. This seems unfair and out of keeping with the general purpose of the sales tax.
Unlike the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, it has never been my habit to interject personal matters into my speeches, but that same copy of the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix from which I have just quoted tells me that its editor now lies dead.
I refer to Clifford Sifton. He was my friend. He was a young man in the prime of life, just 34 years of age. He leaves behind him a widow and four little children. Clifford Sifton was a good newspaper man. He wrote with depth, with feeling and with lightness in his touch. He possessed intellectual honesty to a high degree. He was gentle. He loved the things of nature and the out-of-doors, and was an admirer of good horseflesh. He was a patron of the arts; he loved music and painting and the drama. He raised the cultural level of the community in which he lived, and he will be missed. Now that he has gone our hearts go out in sympathy to those who have most reason to mourn his going.
Now a word or two about the budget itself. The reaction of the public to the budget is proving to be one of disappointment. The first headlines featured a reduction of 11 per cent in the income tax all across the board, but that is now being assessed at its real value. In the first place, the proper figure for the current year is not 11 per cent; it is 5-5 per cent or less. Even that figure sounds impressive until one begins to examine what the reduction means to him personally or on a family basis.
The minister will know the exact figure, but I believe 60 or 70 per cent of our working force pay no income tax at all. They do not earn enough to bring them within the income taxpaying brackets. For those people there is no relief in this budget. Unfortunately there is little relief for those people in the low income bracket by reason of other provisions in the budget.

The Budget-Mr. Knight
These are the men who spend all their income on food, clothing and shelter. We feel that these people should have had some share in the relief from taxation by means of a reduction in the sales tax. The sales tax is a hidden tax and for that reason is all the more insidious. It is a general tax because everybody pays it. It is upon this low income group that the sales tax and special excise taxes bear most heavily, and the government has granted no relief in this connection.
Those in the lower income brackets who Eire well enough off to pay some income tax are in very little better position. We have heard a lot about the married taxpayer with two children, earning $3,000 a year. This year of 1953 that taxpayer will pay just $4 less to the government than he did last year. So far as he is concerned, that is a reduction of 33 cents per month.
I see the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet (Mr. Lesage) is paying attention to what I am saying. I must be fair and say that government speakers have reminded us that the people in the low income groups to which I have just referred who pay no income tax cannot expect any reduction in income tax. Those speakers have pointed out also that these people received benefits in the way of the 4-cent reduction on a package of cigarettes and the abolition of the radio licence fee which cost them $2.50 a year, if they paid it at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And family allowances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The family allowance payments do not buy as much as they used to. It is true that in the two cases I have mentioned there is some relief to many people in the low income group, but there is no relief for the man who makes his own cigarettes or who is a pipe smoker or, I am reminded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), for the non-smoker. These people get no benefit at all.
As to the radio licence fee, that was a nuisance. It was too hard to collect and administer. We are glad to be rid of it. Of course we will still have to pay the special excise tax on the radio in respect of which we used to pay this licence fee. But the nonsmoker receives nothing in this budget for himself or his family. We still have taxes on household goods; we still have excise taxes on refrigerators and kitchen equipment, and there is still the sales tax on candy bars for the children. They all remain the same. What sunshine there is in this budget I submit is not for the workingman.
Of course we are accustomed to that attitude on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). We remember his refusal in


the face of a vote in this house to abolish or lower substantially the deductions for income tax purposes in connection with medical expenses. We remember the ceiling that was placed on contributions for old age security. People with small incomes must pay an extra 2 per cent on their taxable income. But there is a limit of $60 on that 2 per cent tax. A man with taxable income of $3,000 pays 2 per cent or $60. If his taxable income is over $4,000, he still pays $60. If he has a taxable income of $30,000, he still pays only $60 in respect of the old age security tax. That does not seem a fair arrangement to those who believe in the philosophy in which we in this group believe.
People with moderate incomes have been in the habit of putting, and up to now have been encouraged to put, their savings in government bonds. A man with a moderate income may be able to save a few dollars and he does not want to invest it as risk capital. He has been encouraged by this same Minister of Finance to put his money into government bonds. The government has spent a good deal of money in advertising these bonds and telling people that it is a patriotic duty to invest their money in government bonds. But by one stroke in this budget the minister destroys any advantage that there was in that practice. There is a complete change in policy. A man with a few hundred or few thousand dollars invested in government bonds must pay income tax upon the interest received from those bonds. But if he is receiving dividends from Canadian corporations he has been allowed to deduct 10 per cent of those dividends, not from his gross income for taxation purposes but from the amount of tax he is liable to pay. By this budget that exemption is raised from 10 to 20 per cent.
Is it any wonder that people are not buying bonds any more? It will be no wonder if they buy less in the future. The minister is discouraging investment in his own government bonds and encouraging risk capital speculation. The examples given by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), as reported on page 2350 of Hansard of February 24, as to how holders of corporation stock are being favoured are almost incredible. He gave an example of two men, one who earned his income by working, by his effort, perhaps by the practise of his profession, and the other who received income in dividends from his holdings in corporations. Each man is married and has two children. The man whose income consists purely of corporation dividends can have an income as high as $10,000 without having to pay one cent of

*taxes, and that to me is the most remarkable feature about the budget. He pays absolutely nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The tax has been paid.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Private Bills
The minister could have raised the income tax exemptions for the lower income groups but, as I said, we would hardly expect that from a minister who refused to abolish the 4 per cent floor on medical expenses for the purpose of income tax deduction. With the $250 million we have heard so much about the government could have made a nice start on a national health plan.
I am well aware that I am pouring all this into unsympathetic ears. I am well aware that what I am advocating has to do with humanity and social security, and that the government has made a distinct turn-away from these things in the present budget. Bloated with its self-assurance, with its length of time in office, with the inflation of a war economy, it has declared itself for risk capital, capital gains, monopoly capital. If there are those who get in the path of this juggernaut, that is their misfortune.

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 187, respecting a certain patent and patent application of Florence F. Loudon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: It may be the pleasure of the house to adopt it later, but we would like to know the reasons why we should.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: My hon. friend will be glad to accommodate you.

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the title of the bill indicates, the subject matter has to do with the restoration of an application for a patent. In May of 1945 the applicant, Mrs. Florence F. Loudon, conceived the idea of an arrangement for hanging overcurtains in such a way that they could be released from the valance without having to go to the great trouble of removing the hooks. She and her husband decided to make a model of this appliance, and they consulted a patent attorney in the city of Toronto. He suggested that it would be advisable for them to submit an application to both the Canadian patent office and the United States patent office. The application was drafted in November, 1945, and submitted to the Canadian patent office. After two or three months Mrs. Loudon consulted the patent attorney, who advised her that it took between two and four years to acquire a patent of this kind.

She was a lady without business experience of any kind, and her husband had little business experience.
The matter went on until 1949 before she received any definite report from her attorney. In July of that year he reported to her and advised that the United States patent office had refused her application. She was somewhat alarmed about the evasive answers which she had received from her patent attorney so she wrote a letter direct to the patent office and was advised by them that the patent office had objected to the application but that the objection had been made on April 17, 1947; that no reply had been received to the report made by the patent office, and consequently her application had been abandoned.
She consulted another patent attorney asking him what course she should follow. He looked over her material and advised her that, as there was some difference between the invention and the material which had been placed on file, she should submit another application to the United States patent office.
About the same time that she consulted her second patent attorney she asked him to inquire about the status of her Canadian patent. He advised her that the report from the Canadian patent office had not been replied to and, consequently, the application for Canadian patent had also been abandoned. However, he advised her to go ahead with a subsequent application. At that time he did not find it advisable to inform her that if she had manufactured and sold a certain number of these appliances it would prejudice her position with respect to her patent application. Finally, it was necessary for her to consult another solicitor. He informed her that the proper way by which to straighten out the predicament in which she found herself was to ask for a private bill permitting her to proceed with her original application.
Mrs. Loudon now takes that position, which is considered by her solicitors to be the only possible course open to her to retrieve her original position, placing herself in the same position as if she had originally started and made application for patent of her invention. The effect of this bill if passed will simply be to put Mrs. Loudon in the position in which she would have been had her original patent attorney not been derelict in his duty and failed to answer the report made by the Canadian examiner in the first place. The bill provides that she should surrender any existing patent and authorize the commissioner, on such surrender and upon the making of a reply within two months of the passing of the

act, to proceed with the original application as if it had not been abandoned.
If the bill is passed Mrs. Loudon will acquire no greater rights with respect to her application than if she had been applying in due time on the original report of July 8, 1947. In view of the difficulties with which this lady has been confronted on two previous occasions, it is my submission that she should be relieved of the situation in which she finds herself by the passing of this private bill, in order that she might patent her invention in the hope that it may be a worth-while scheme to carry out the manufacture of this product.

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say very much on this bill except that there is no suggestion, in this house anyway, that any delays or hardships suffered were due to inefficiency or conditions in the patent office.

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext: Is everything all right there?

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext:
I have had the opportunity of practising before the patent office for-and I hate to say it-24 years. I must admit that at present the conditions of work and the results achieved by the patent office are much better than they have ever been in the past 24 or 25 years. That is due to the fact that the staff has been increased; there are more technical men on the staff; and I think it is due also to the fact that there are more capable patent attorneys practising before the patent office today. At one time anybody was an attorney before the patent office who chose to practice there.
I understand that the gentleman who acted as attorney in the first case was a little bit derelict, and it is unfortunate for the inventor that she should have suffered so. I would only point out one thing, however, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this bill, and it is that there are a great many cases where attorneys or inventors themselves have not replied to reports of the patent office within six months and their cases have been abandoned. They might now plead ignorance, and that they did not have advice regarding a delay of only six months. We might have a great number of these bills coming before us from people who have the money to pay for a private bill. That is not the reason I object to this particular case which has its merits, but I wish to make it clear in this case that there is no attack justified on the staff of the patent office. They are efficient, they are doing a good honest job, and I wish to pay them that tribute as it is deserved.

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext:
I have no intention of making an attack on the Canadian patent office.
Private Bills

subtopic: PATENT APPLICATION OF FLORENCE F. LOUDON
speechtext:
I am not saying that. I am not speaking about this house but what happened in the other place a few days ago.
I suggest also that if the patent office practice was amended a little, what has happened in this case would not happen so often. I think the patent office could well send a duplicate of these notices-as they do in the trade mark office-to the inventor as well as to the attorney . If the inventor were to receive a duplicate of the notice and report sent to the attorney, then the inventor would not have any reason to complain later that he had not been advised of the proceedings before the patent office. It would mean very little work on the part of the patent office, and it is general practice in connection with trade marks. I think we would avoid the reception of such bills as this if the patent office were to take notice of the suggestion I am making now.
There is another point I would make. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kinders-ley (Mr. Larson) who is sponsoring this bill has not given the house a complete explanation of the purpose of the parties who are applying for this charter. In effect, the only thing he has said is that if they get the charter they intend to build a gas pipe line from Alberta through different Saskatchewan centres to Manitoba; and then he said something to the effect that they intend to go on to eastern Canada. I must admit at the commencement of my remarks that if I really believed that was the intention of the applicants, I would have little objection to this bill. But because I do not think that is as yet their real intention, I propose to make a few remarks with regard to the bill.
This bill is almost identical with one which was introduced by the same hon. member in the session of 1952. That bill sought the


incorporation of a company to be known as Boundary Pipeline Corporation. As hon. members know, it did not pass the house, and died with the ending of the session.
It is true there are some changes in the present bill, one of which is the name. The company it was hoped to incorporate last year was to be known as the Boundary Pipeline Corporation. This year when the applicants for incorporation went before the other place they asked for the incorporation of a company to be known as Canadian Pipelines Limited. However, in the other place that name was changed to MidContinent Pipelines Limited; and we now have this latter name in the bill we are considering.
The second change is that whereas in the bill last year power was sought to construct pipe lines within the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, or outside Canada, this year the bill contains the words "within or outside Canada". There is no reference to the three provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
There is one other change in that in the present bill we find a provision to the effect that the main line shall be constructed entirely within Canada. A similar provision was written into last year's bill, in committee; but unfortunately that provision does not mean very much, if anything, where a pipe line company proposes to run its line down to the United States boundary, and then sell the gas to an associate company incorporated under the laws of the United States.
The provision is of some effect in the cases we dealt with in the house in 1949 and 1950, where it was intended to run a pipe line west from Alberta down into the United States at the nearest convenient point, through the states and then back into Canada. There, a provision to the effect that the main line was to be entirely within Canada did meet our objection, which was that we wanted the line to be built in Canada. In a plan such as I believe that of the sponsors of the present bill to be, namely getting their gas into the United States south of Winnipeg, such a provision is of no value.
During the sittings of the committee last year I asked counsel appearing for the applicants, Mr. Duncan K. MacTavish, Q.C., a question to be found at page 8 of the proceedings of the committee. I said:
Of course by saying that the main line would be in Canada; in saying that you are going on the basis that that would not prevent them making a deal with an American company to export gas?
And he answered:
Yes, I think that would be a fair thing to say, Mr. Green.

But while there are these differences in the bill as presented this year the applicants are the same individuals who applied last year. Furthermore I believe that the people who are behind these applicants are the same people who were behind the bill presented in 1952. They were listed in the other place, and one of them was stated to be the Fish Engineering Corporation of Houston, Texas. In effect that company was the main applicant for a charter last year, and I believe is the main applicant behind this present bill.
It is worth noting that this same corporation, the Fish Engineering Corporation of Houston, Texas, is today putting up a very bitter battle before the United States federal power commission to prevent the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited from taking Peace river gas into the northwest states.
The very company which comes here now asking for this charter is trying to prevent Peace river gas going into the states of Washington and Oregon. It is doing so through another subsidiary, known as the Pacific Northwest Pipe Line Corporation.
These hearings have been going on before the federal power commission, and may very well end in preventing Canadian gas from going into the northwest states.

On a point of order, I am
sure this is not a subsidiary of the Fish Engineering Corporation.

Well, I have here a report of the speech in the other place, where the sponsor said, as reported at page 249 of the official report of debates of the Senate:
In addition to the men named in the petition, others interested in the company will be-
And then, following other names we find this:
-and Fish Engineering Company, Houston, Texas, who will be in charge of technical development.
This is the same corporation that was behind the bill last year. And I believe that, just as last year, the main purpose of this group is to take Canadian gas from the prairies down into the United States, and particularly to the state of Minnesota.
I have here a copy of the petition they presented to the House of Commons in seeking this charter. It sets out the powers and objects they request, one of which is to purchase, distribute and sell natural and artificial gas and oil within Canada and, if required, to export the same to the United States. The very fact that the name has been changed to Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited indicates that that is where they really intend to do business.
Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited
Last year there were several grounds for opposition to the granting of the charter. One was that the applicants proposed to build an extremely small pipe line, only 16 inches in diameter. The sponsor of this bill has not mentioned the size proposed in 1953. There were objections to such a plan because it was pointed out that so small a pipe line could not possibly operate on an economic basis. As a result there would have to be a second pipe line laid down beside the first, thereby running up the cost to the consumer and probably cutting down the price received by the supplier.
Another objection last year to the incorporation was that the applicants had no gas whatever on the prairie. Unlike other pipeline companies, these applicants had no gas of their own. Furthermore, they had done nothing or very little by way of survey. It was admitted before the house committee that they had spent only $25,000 in making preparations, whereas other applicants for pipe-line charters had spent into the hundreds of thousands of dollars in nearly every case.
I believe it was felt last year by many members of the house that these applicants were merely trying to get a charter for its nuisance value. If they could get a charter and then by hook or crook get permission to export gas from Alberta ahead of other pipe-line companies, they would be in position to call the tune. There would be no doubt that they would have a most valuable asset. I believe the same position exists today with these applicants applying again for a charter. Another ground on which we opposed the application last year was that the gas was to be taken to the United States.
These grounds of opposition are equally valid at the present time, particularly the last objection that the applicants intend to take the gas to the United States. I say that is a valid ground of opposition on the broad basis of national policy. The year 1953 is crucial in so far as the exportation of gas from Alberta to the east is concerned. This is the year when we all expect that a decision will be made by the Alberta petroleum and natural gas conservation board and subsequently by the Alberta government to the effect that gas can be exported east from that province.
For some years Alberta was unwilling to allow any gas to be exported, but just about a year ago the conservation board gave permission for the export of gas to the west coast from the Peace river field. Apparently that was done on the basis that gas from the field would not be available for export to the east; that this field could not be used

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited conveniently as a source of gas for the east. In the hope of developing the Peace river country and selling gas down the west coast, the conservation board and the provincial government of Alberta consented to the export of gas from the Peace river area.
The government of British Columbia has been in favour of such export throughout. Actually at the present time there are greater gas reserves in the British Columbia portion of the Peace river country than there are in the Alberta portion. Hon. members will be interested to know that Dr. George
S.	Hume, the Canadian expert on oil and natural gas, and a very highly respected civil servant, pointed out last summer that in his opinion there was a greater supply of gas in the Fort St. John district than there appeared to be in any other western field, including Pincher Creek.
After the Alberta conservation board and the Alberta government had consented to the export of gas to the west coast, the board of transport commissioners here in Ottawa gave their consent and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) issued a permit to the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited for the export of gas to Washington and Oregon, or in any event his department gave a clear indication that such a permit would be available. So the export of Alberta gas to the west coast was decided last year.
It seems clear now in 1953 that there is sufficient gas in southern Alberta for export to the east, but the difficulty is that there is not sufficient to supply Ontario, Montreal and possibly Quebec city and at the same time supply Minnesota. It may be interesting to hon. members to know that Minnesota already is receiving some Texas gas, but apparently they would also like to get gas from Alberta.

Has the hon. member
figures to show that Alberta has not sufficient to supply these markets?

I do not have the figures and the decision has not yet been given by the Alberta conservation board. But I understand it is generally believed that sufficient reserves have been developed in Alberta to justify the export of gas to the east. I hope I am not wrong in that belief.

I think the hon. member might probably expect to find that the next decision of the conservation board will be more optimistic than the one given previously due to the fact that such tremendous discoveries of oil have been made.

There have been many large discoveries, both in southern Alberta and in the Peace river district. To come back to

my point, if Alberta gas is to go to Minnesota then it is clear that none will come east of Winnipeg for a long time. Therefore we find that the question at the present time is whether Alberta gas is to go to central Canada or to Minnesota. Nineteen hundred and fifty-three is the year of decision. That is why this application now before us is of such importance, for it raises the whole question.
As the house knows, I am strongly in favour of gas going to Ontario and Quebec by an all-Canadian route. I do not care what company puts in the line. One company, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, offers to do so, and if that company can construct a line there is no reason why others could not do it. It should be pointed out that no matter what company constructs the line, it will be done by private enterprise. These pipe-line builders are prepared to find the money and carry through the work.
If gas were brought east to Ontario and Quebec by an all-Canadian route it would serve Kenora, the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur and the north shore of lake Superior where new industries are being established each year and where natural gas would be of great benefit. It would also serve the city of Sudbury where we have the district that provides most of the nickel produced in the world. It would probably also serve northern Ontario. Then there would be storage in the old wells of southwestern Ontario and dozens of centres in southern Ontario, and Montreal and possibly the city of Quebec would be served by this all-Canadian pipe line.
The benefits from such a plan can only be described as stupendous. In the first place the cost would be from $270 to $300 million, which would mean hundreds and perhaps thousands of jobs for Canadians. There would be no question of control of any part of the gas line by the United States. Alberta would have a pipe line of adequate size to ensure the taking away of available gas, and would have a steady market in central Canada. Saskatchewan and Manitoba would be helped in similar fashion. Another result would be the opening of new gas and oil wells in those two prairie provinces, both of which have great prospects for such development.
In Ontario there would be great benefits. Take,	for example, northwestern and
northern Ontario. There is the possibility of gas being used for smelting purposes at Sudbury. It is to be used at Fort Saskatchewan in Alberta to smelt nickel ore from the Lynn Lake mine in northern Manitoba. A smelter is being built there of a value of

over $17 million, and I suggest there are great possibilities for a similar use for natural gas in the Sudbury area. Dr. Hume, to whom I referred a few minutes ago, delivered a speech on May 9, 1951 before the engineering institute of Canada on the subject "The Utilization of Natural Gas in Canada". He had this to say with regard to the benefits to northern Ontario to be derived from an all-Canadian pipe line:
There is no doubt that the bringing of natural gas across the pre-Cambrian shield of northern Ontario could provide immense benefit to our paper, and more particularly to our mining communities such as Sudbury, Steep Rock and to Fort William, Port Arthur, and perhaps to Sault Ste. Marie, although this is, as far as known, outside the present plans and would have to be considered in relation to the size of the market for the length of pipe line needed to supply it. Northern Ontario, except for wood, is entirely deficient in fuel and the use of natural gas at a moderate price such as a pipe line could supply would be a boon of inestimable value in its development.
In southern Ontario and in the Montreal and Quebec areas natural gas would mean a cheaper, more dependable and cleaner fuel than coal which has to be imported from the United States. It means additional power for industry which will be so badly needed for many years in southern Ontario and the Montreal area if they are to continue their development of recent times. Dr. Hume had something to say ip the same speech concerning the use of natural gas. He said:
Natural gas for heating has a number of advantages over fuel oil, and indeed of all fuels in common use today, it most nearly approaches the ideal. Its high heat value, about double that of manufactured gas made from coal, gives it a great advantage where a supply is available and whereas for domestic use the burning of fuel oil is dependent upon electricity for blower operation, the use of natural gas is dependent alone upon the maintenance of a small pressure in the distribution mains.
He goes on to say:
To many people vaguely familiar with the use of natural gas its advantages are little appreciated, but to engineers who understand the efficient consumption of fuels no exhaustive statements of its comparative values are needed. It can be taken for granted that, given a selection at comparable prices, the public would choose natural gas above all other forms of fuel, especially for the heating of dwellings, and where natural gas was available in quantity it would be the choice also for many commercial and industrial purposes.
One of the great weaknesses in the Canadian economy, Mr. Speaker, has been the dependence of Ontario and Quebec on United States coal. The other day figures were brought down in the house which are to be found at page 2384 of Hansard for February 25. They show that the tonnage of coal brought into Canada from the United States last year amounted to 24,576,821 tons.
