speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate for the purpose of bringing to the attention of parliament a matter which may not have national characteristics to some of those who may be listening, but it very definitely is a national issue to the people of Clarkson, Lome Park, Port Credit, Dixie and Lakeview. For those whose geography has failed them for the moment, I refer to the vicinity of south Peel. In bringing the problems of the railway commuters to parliament I think I ought to mention that it is not the first time these problems have been before parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Nor is it the first time they have been discussed both in a general and a particular way in other circles as well.
I might point out first of all that this problem of railway commuter service has been a vexing problem for many years not only in the Toronto area but in other metropolitan areas as well. However, it is only the metropolitan area of Toronto and its adjoining sections that I desire to cover in my arguments tonight. Also I think I ought to point out to the membership of the house that the south end of the county of Peel has trebled in population in the period which began in the 1940's. That growth has continued rapidly since that time. We have there now a city of 30,000 people and an area that is growing day by day in a most spectacular fashion.
Many of the people who have come to south Peel came from the city of Toronto. Many of them are still working in the city of Toronto, but they have their homes in the new residential sections which have been developed in our county. We welcome those people, of course, and some of the finest citizens have come to reside there. Many people have just set up their homes and are engaged in business or other work in the city or its environs.
This has, of course, provided some problems in traffic and transportation that did not exist before. Despite wide highways, like the Queen Elizabeth highway and others that traverse the area, the eight o'clock to nine-thirty bottleneck in the mornings for those

coming into Toronto from the west is only too familiar to those who know the locality well for me to enlarge upon it on an occasion such as this; but the motor traffic bottleneck at the Humber bridge at the west entrance to Toronto is very little short of a scandal so far as general traffic is concerned. In connection with that bottleneck, may I say that that situation is not confined entirely to the entrance to Toronto or to the entrance to any particular city. All these bottlenecks with respect to motor traffic, of course, result from the fact that a good many people have moved into the suburbs and now use automobiles to get to their work in Toronto, Montreal or elsewhere. That being the case, of course, it is understandable that even with wide, modern highways such as the Queen Elizabeth and others, traffic into the cities is greatly congested.
It is at this point, of course, that the importance of the railway commuter service becomes evident. I think it may be said that this part of the county of Peel has developed to a point where I think it is abreast or perhaps ahead of most similar sections of the country which are close to metropolitan cities. I believe it may be said that we are abreast of all the developments that are occurring, but we are very sadly behind when it comes to the question of commutation railway services, and those necessities which are now showing themselves in the transportation field. Of course the commuters' service has increased in importance because of the conditions I have mentioned, and which are so prevalent in the general suburban scheme of things.
In the midst of this congested traffic picture one finds traversing that area to which I have just drawn attention two main trunk lines of railway. One is the Canadian National from Toronto to Hamilton and the other is the Canadian Pacific Railway, which has running rights over these tracks. The Canadian Pacific trains do not stop at intermediate points, but only stop at Toronto and Hamilton and then go on to Buffalo. This line is known as the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo line. The Canadian National Railways from Toronto to Hamilton largely handles the commutation traffic; in fact this line handles all the commuters between Toronto and Oakville.
I might point out that there is a commutation rate structure which covers tickets from Toronto to Oakville, a distance of about 21 miles, and the intervening points. This rate structure covers Clarkson, Lome Park, Port Credit, Dixie, Lakeview and places closer to Toronto. The Canadian National daily takes care of about 1,000 passengers who are travelling on that commutation scale. There should

be a lot more people travelling under that commutation arrangement, and if we had the kind of service we should have I am quite certain that the highway traffic, which is so congested as I have explained before, would be greatly relieved by this railway transportation.
It is hard to believe that the type of equipment used on that road would be used on a line which is perhaps the most heavily travelled railway trackage in the whole Dominion of Canada. Those of you who have attempted to cross this railway line will have found that every few minutes a heavy train goes by in one direction or the other. In the midst of this heavy railway traffic through Toronto on the Canadian National line, I think it ought to be pointed out that on these commuter trains we have twelve wooden coaches. These twelve wooden coaches were built about the time when the Yukon gold rush was at its height. This gives one some idea of the antiquated equipment that is employed in that service. As was pointed out in debates in this house some years ago, these coaches are good material for match boxes and kindling, in the event of even a minor accident. It is easy to understand that, even with the electrically controlled block system, there is the danger of an accident in the midst of this heavy traffic.
At the same time one finds in these cars a lighting arrangement which I fancy is the most antiquated in Canada. It is gas lighting, with all the attendant fire hazards. It is dangerous to health because every so often the light goes out and the gas escapes. The result is that not only is there low candle-power for the people who are using the lights, but there is a danger to health as well. In addition to that there is poor ventilation, probably as poor as there is in the whole country. The trains are crowded and there is every possible kind of inconvenience from that source. Perhaps I need not mention it, but in addition to that there are no adequate heat controls.
This whole situation makes for a lack of accommodation and convenience which can hardly be imagined for that type of service. I am told by a reliable source-this has not been contradicted by the railway-that between 10 and 15 people have to stand in [DOT]every coach going in and out every day. This means that something like between 100 and 150 people never get a seat from the time they get on the train until they get into Toronto.
Added to all this is the fact that the train schedules have never been changed during all these years, while the working hours of many people in the metropolitan centre of Toronto
The Budget-Mr. Graydon have been changed. One realizes that when a train comes in at eight-thirty in the morning, as No. 79 does, it means that there are some people who do not arrive in time for work. For that reason it is an inconvenient hour for some people. I suppose, however, that for a good many it is still as good an hour as they can ask for under the circumstances.
One of the troubles is that the train does not always arrive on time. There is a disposition from time to time on the part of these trains not to keep to the timetable too closely. I think one ought to mention also that when the train arrives at Union station there is a clutter of express, baggage and congestion from other trains, and this constitutes one of the main sources of complaints that the commuters have.
One of the problems, of course, is this. In addition to all the inconveniences that are suffered there and the fact that many of these people have come out from the city expecting at least to have some semblance of accommodation for their commuting into Toronto, I think the situation now constitutes a more intense problem than it has ever constituted at any time in the past.
These matters have been raised time and again by interested parties. I was at a meeting of railway officials and many of the commuters on January 5 of this year in the offices of the Canadian National Railways in Toronto. There the matter was gone over carefully and some promises were made to the effect that in 1954 we were going to get some relief with respect to the type of trains, or the type of coaches; that we were going to get a better lighting system and a better ventilating system; and that, in addition, they would look over the question of the timetables.
One of the things that struck me in connection with the matter-and it was one of the reasons I wanted to raise the matter in the house-was that the Canadian National Railways seem to be extremely diffident about dealing with this matter until they are pressed into some kind of action. I do not mind saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that I am satisfied that one of the reasons the Canadian National Railways finally moved part way toward a settlement of this matter was that in the local newspapers, in the metropolitan newspapers of Toronto and in one of the United States news magazines, these matters began to take form and began to roll up into a heavy snowball of criticism against the railway. It was only when that criticism reached its height that the commuters began to be recognized at all in that area. They had written letters; representations had been made, but it was not until the
2588	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Graydon spotlight of publicity was turned on the railway that any action came at all. I think it is unfortunate that the commuters should have had to depend upon the fact that certain other people had raised voices on their behalf. I think it is unfortunate that the railways did not long ago recognize their plight and do something about it before they were forced, by public opinion, into the position of doing something in connection with the matter.
I might mention one or two of these matters so far as the local newspapers are concerned. In the largely circulated Port Credit Weekly, which is published in that area, reference is made to the matter in an editorial of November 6, 1952. In an open letter to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) the editorial goes on to say:
We've got two things to "beef" about. One is the quality of equipment used on commuter trains between this area and Toronto, and the other is the whistle-blowing locomotives that speed through this area every fifteen minutes or so.
And it goes on to say:
Reading accounts of a recent Ontario train wreck, we noticed that one train had two express cars as a "buffer" between the passenger coaches and the engine, while the other had three "buffer" cars. Had it not been for this cushion, the wreck would have been much more serious and the death toll tremendous.
Regular travellers on commuter runs between south Peel communities and Toronto tell us that these trains have only one "buffer" car between the locomotive and the 12 passenger coaches. Since these trains are nearly always jammed to capacity, it is quite obvious that each train is carrying 800 to 1,000 people each trip.
If two or three "buffer" cars are deemed necessary on a regular passenger train with modern steel cars, we would think many more "buffers" would be required on commuter trains with their antiquated wooden coaches.
I want also to read into the record, if I may, one or two excerpts which I think have been well chosen in their language and which perhaps might assist us in recognizing the problem. One is from the Globe and Mail of November 26, 1952, from an article written by Lex Schrag entitled "Growing Pains

See Trains Solution for Suburbs". This is what Mr. Schrag says:
While the Ontario municipal board is still diagnosing greater Toronto's growing pains on the basis of the city's application for amalgamation nearly three years ago, new symptoms of transportation ailments are becoming manifest.
The railways have been cool towards suggestions of commuter services. Such services are operated from Oakville and Weston into city stations. Now, with development of the big Ford plant at Oakville, two-way commuter service will be needed.
Admittedly, the Ford factory will have ample employee parking space. But whether the Queen Elizabeth way will carry the load of two-way traffic that can develop from further industrial expansion in the lakeshore area remains to be seen . . .


While suburban residents have more influence with local councils than with the T.T.C. in obtaining such services, neither council nor the commission is going to underwrite the type of service which would lure prospective customers away from the use of their own autos. Therefore, car transportation continues to be worth its greater cost to the suburbanite.
Since public transportation is inextricably mixed with private means of locomotion-at least until the subway begins to operate-the motor car will continue to carry an uneconomic proportion of suburban traffic.
Finally, however, motor traffic will strangle itself and the existing forms of public transport at the same time. Then, the railways would have to come to the rescue, for the construction of multimillion-dollar highways is slow as well as costly, and would be useless without the equally costly provision of parking facilities.
I want to go further, if I may, and mention also this other matter which I think ought to be stressed. This is from a commuter himself who has taken an active part in the campaign to get better service for those who travel on trains from south Peel to Toronto. This is what is said by Mr. W. Leslie Todd in a letter to the Minister of Transport dated November 27, 1952:
The mass movement of working people to and from their places of business, particularly in the larger centres of population, has become an increasingly difficult problem. Automobile and bus highways are rapidly becoming totally inadequate for the task. It is, therefore, in the nation's interests that adequate commuter service be supplied by the one vehicle that can properly move large groups of people-the railroads.
The answer may well be found through the operation of smaller and more frequent commuter trains on the established rail lines leading in and out of densely populated areas. The Montreal picture, possibly because of competing lines, seems to have been given adequate attention already.
Now I should like to add, if I may, to those matters I have already mentioned, a reference made by Mr. Ken W. MacTaggart of the Globe and Mail, who has taken a keen and active interest in this question. I believe he lives at Oakville himself and is a regular commuter to Toronto. As I said, he has taken a keen interest in this matter. Some of his articles which appeared in connection with the commuters' problem in the early part of this last year have done a great deal to help. In one of his articles in the Globe and Mail, on December 5, 1952, he had this to say:
Inauguration of an adequate rail commuter service between Hamilton and Toronto is held by transportation officials as a logical solution of the traffic problems of the lakeshore district west of Toronto, where population has expanded at a rate far in excess of the rest of the metropolitan area.
During a period when Oakville, Port Credit, Clarkson, Lome Park and the townships of Trafalgar and Toronto have doubled and trebled their populations of Toronto commuters, railway transportation has not improved. In some ways it has declined. Recently, however, commuters have been given hopes than an improvement might come, with announcement by the C.N.R. that new de luxe

equipment was being acquired for Montreal's commuter trains . . . Ontario's highways officials would be happy to see commuter trains helping to take part of the load that is now jamming the westerly routes into the city every day. The trams would also, in the opinion of city officials, help keep cars out of the city, thus easing the strain on parking facilities.
Added to that, of course, have been from time to time the very strenuous campaigns waged by the Oakville-Trafalgar Journal, which has taken a special interest in seeing that the problems of the commuters are solved in some way. Their editorials and news articles have been most effective during the time this campaign has been at its height.
The present position is that we have received some promises that something will be done at some time in 1954. But the one feature that is still confusing the people in the south Peel area is that even though some of these improvements have been promised by the railways, and may be carried out, the fact still remains that we have a commuters' service inferior to comparable areas outside the city of Montreal.
I am not for one moment suggesting that the suburban areas of Montreal should not have the kind of service they do have. Indeed, I should like to see them have even better service, if possible. I refer to Montreal only to show the contrast. I would mention particularly, for instance, the railway passenger train service from Ste. Annes into Montreal, where there are no less than two railways competing, both the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. While there are six commuters' trains available for people travelling from Ste. Annes to Montreal each morning, there are only two trains serving the area between Oakville, Port Credit and points in south Peel and Toronto.

speechtext:
No, I should think they are not. When you realize that there are six trains going from Ste. Annes and only two from Oakville, there can be no doubt that what my hon. friend says is perfectly right.
It seems to me that, despite the fact that the head office of the Canadian National Railways happens to be in Montreal, the railway management should not lose sight of the fact that there is a rapidly growing community in the south Peel and lakeshore areas outside Toronto. I suggest they are not receiving the kind of railway transportation service they ought to have. They want a faster, more commodious and more frequent service.
We must approach the problem always having in mind the new directions in which these suburbs are developing. There is no doubt in my mind that the easiest way to bring those
The Budget-Mr. Graydon people to the very heart and core of the business centres of metropolitan areas is, so far as possible, to bring them by train. This does not pose a parking problem, nor does it bring about bottlenecks at the entrance to the western, eastern or northern city gates. It brings the people to work comfortably, if the railway cars are brought up to date.
I believe this problem has never been properly tackled, and it is one that every metropolitan area in Canada will have to tackle at some time. I suggest it should be done now. The need is great, and the railways should work out some system whereby, in great measure, they will be able to relieve the monstrous traffic jams in which the motorists now find themselves night and morning travelling to and from their work.
I remember discussing this matter about two years ago with several people, as to the relative values of taking one's car to work or going by train. At that time, having canvassed the subject through discussions with half a dozen people who travel back and forth constantly, I found that nearly all of them said they would prefer to go by motorcar because, in so doing, they could park their cars near their work, could carry some friends to and from work, and thereby reduce the cost. After two years, however, with traffic becoming so congested, each of those persons has said he would prefer to get on a commuter train and be taken to work by the railways. It must be kept in mind that this congestion has developed to a greater extent in the last couple of years than it had in the preceding ten years.
I think it will be found that in metropolitan areas throughout Canada the move is afoot to bring commuters by the railways, thus benefiting both the suburban areas and the cities. I believe the railways regard the commuter service as a nuisance, and they are convinced that they lose money on it. They feel that if there is some way whereby they could get out of the business altogether they would be greatly pleased. The result is that they are doing as little as possible for this service, commensurate with keeping behind them a certain amount of public opinion. Their hope is, no doubt, that in the end they will freeze out the commuter service and mark it off their books.
In my view that is a shortsighted way of dealing with it. A new deal for commuters in metropolitan areas is long overdue. I should like to see the matter tackled on a common-sense basis whereby the railway commuter service would be worked in with the general plan of growth and development of our suburban and metropolitan areas.

The Budget-Mr. Parent
Tomorrow in the Ontario legislature a major development for the Toronto area is to be discussed. While this is a move toward a certain goal, I think it would be a great shame if the question of railway transportation service were not coupled with the other factors which go to make up a great metropolitan area and its adjacent areas. I plead with the railways, the government and all who may be interested in this subject to try to work out some system whereby there may be easier access by railway than by motorcar, realizing that by using the railways we will be helping to relieve a present difficulty.
Before taking my seat may I suggest that a survey should be made touching other points connected with this commuter service. It is a patchwork, jigsaw puzzle plan at the present time. Oakville, which is about a tenth of a mile farther away from Toronto than Brampton, has commutation rates while Brampton has not. Malton, which has become one of the great industrial centres, has no commutation rates although it is much closer to Toronto than Oakville. I am not quite so familiar with the municipalities east of Toronto, but the same situation prevails there.
It seems to me that these municipalities should not have to go to the expense of appearing before the railway board to fight their cases simply because the railway companies are reluctant to provide the service. The railway companies always have high-powered legal men to plead their cases. Brampton has appeared before the board on one or two occasions, and I would not be surprised if it appears again in the immediate future. A survey of the whole area is essential. Commutation rates should be set for places like Streetsville, Brampton, Malton and other municipalities east of Toronto so they can get the service they deserve.
I know that to many members who come from other parts of Canada these problems may seem far away from their own problems, but all of us have our particular problems in our particular parts of Canada. It would be a great shame if we were not able to localize these issues which actually are national to the people at home and which should receive national attention in this national parliament.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to thank the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) for having taken us for such a ride without anybody getting hurt. He has presented a transportation problem to this house, and as he is a very popular member I am sure his remarks will receive the best possible consideration.
I do not intend to take up very much time, and I will limit my remarks to that part of

the budget address of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in which he invited a greater participation in equity ownership in order to have the Canadian people participate in the industrial wealth of this country. That was wise advice and worthy of our great Minister of Finance. I had the privilege of coming to this house at the same time he did. Although I have grown older it seems that the more the minister works, the younger he gets. I am sure everyone will agree that he is one of the great ministers of finance Canada has had.
Undoubtedly it is to the benefit of all to participate in one way or another in building up our country. For some years I have been bringing to the attention of the authorities the lack of information given to shareholders by various companies. I believe the time has come to look into this matter. Because of the wealth of our country and the expansion that has taken place, in my opinion this is a major issue.
The value of the stocks listed on the Toronto stock exchange is $15 billion, while those listed on the Montreal stock exchange have a total valuation of $13 billion. The federal Companies Act has become outmoded. To use an expression used by the hon. member for Peel, it belongs in the days of the Yukon, in the days of the horse and buggy.
The investment dealers' association, the Canadian institute of chartered accountants and the association of Canadian advertisers investigated 700 companies in Canada and found that less than one-quarter went to the trouble of providing sufficient information to their shareholders in order that they might know if their money was being handled in a fair and equitable way.
I should like to give a few examples of what is going on in this country. The Minister of Finance has made an appeal to the public to invest money in Canadian enterprises, but I do not think one should do so unless he is sure that his money is being properly managed. I should like to quote an article which appeared in the Financial Post of January 6, 1951, as follows:
Why Should Companies Report on Subsidiaries?
Why should all companies issue a consolidated annual report or else separate annual reports for each of their subsidiaries? A good reason is seen in financial circles this week.
In the prospectus covering the offering of 319,548 common shares of Canada Iron Foundries Ltd., a consolidated balance sheet at Sept. 30, 1950 and a consolidated statement of the earnings of the company and its subsidiaries for the 10 years and nine months ended Sept. 30, 1950 are shown. These present a much better and more complete picture of the financial position of the company than the shareholders-the owners of the business-have

heretofore been able to obtain from the annual reports, which have been on a parent company only basis.
For example, total assets at Sept. 30, 1950 are shown at $21,597,192 on a consolidated basis as compared with $11,413,896 at Dec. 31, 1949 in the company's annual report, which carried shares in and amounts owing by subsidiary companies at $3,299,254. Further, the net profit for 1949 (which included dividends from subsidiary companies totalling $445,000) amounted to $728,286 according to the annual report but, according to the prospectus, on a consolidated amount basis amounted to $1,546,384 or over double the figure given to the shareholders previously.
The same applies also to one of the largest and most prosperous companies, which includes on its board of directors leaders of the financial world in Canada. For the first time in the history of that company, when they wanted people to put money into the company and were issuing convertible bonds, they came out with a consolidated balance sheet increasing their assets from $71 million to over $100 million and showing a surplus of nearly $23 million over what was given on the unconsolidated balance sheet. They showed earnings per share of $3.05 on the consolidated basis compared with $1.94 on an unconsolidated basis.
How can you expect people to invest money in companies if they are going to be at the mercy of the few who do not want to give them any information when they attend annual meetings? Most of the time the old answer that has been used for over 50 years is given, that it is not in the interests of the company that it should be divulged. In the United States you at least have consolidated balance sheets and quarterly statements because it is recognized that investing money is a science, and that you cannot invest money properly unless you have the facts.
I believe there should be some such provision in the Companies Act. Last October I had the pleasure of attending a conference of representatives of all provinces except Quebec who came here to discuss amendments to the Companies Act. Briefs were submitted by the Canadian Bar Association and the chartered accountants of Canada. They were unanimous in stating that our Companies Act is outmoded and does not give enough protection to the investor.
When we are just starting to scratch the wealth of this country, when we are opening up the oil fields of the west, when we are opening up the north, the Yukon, Labrador and Newfoundland, when these developments are going to bring money into Canada from the United States, why should we not as Canadians be given an opportunity to participate in these developments and at least let the one who wants to risk his money have the certainty that there is a law upon which $8108-165
The Budget-Mr. Parent he can rely in claiming his right to be told what is being done with his money? I know companies that have six or seven subsidiaries and the main companies, which are listed on the stock exchange, are practically showing deficits while the subsidiaries are making hundreds of thousands of dollars.
I have no hesitation in mentioning in the house the great Algoma Steel Company which issues an unconsolidated balance sheet from which you cannot get any information about its subsidiaries. Whether Sir James Dunn likes it or not, there are some subsidiaries of Algoma Steel which are making as much money as Algoma Steel itself. Yet this company has not paid any dividends to its shareholders for over 20 years, and I do not believe I am wrong in stating that on the basis of a consolidated balance sheet they would probably show earnings of $10 to $12 per share.
This is the state of affairs in this country. How can you expect people to participate in our industries unless there is a law to protect the investments of our people? Last night William H. Phillips, district superintendent of the Bank of Montreal, in speaking to the Canadian industrial editors' association, said that confusing terms and lack of information in companies' reports should be done away with, and that the people should be brought into the secrets of the companies in order to know how their money is being spent. I have been asking for a change for a long time. I have always thought this was a matter that might not be of interest to the people, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has brought the problem before the house and I congratulate him for doing so because it is absolutely sound that we should own our country before others own us. He should be congratulated on having made such a statement. I believe we should get all the information that is necessary to make sound investments.
As to the budget itself, I remember we were told once that the best way to judge the affairs of the country is to read the financial reports of all the big banking institutions in Canada. We were told they were honestly run and that their boards were composed of prominent Conservatives. If you read the annual reports of the banks this year you will see that they are practically unanimous in certifying that this country is well run and prosperous, that it is run on a sound basis, and that Canada has many great years of prosperity ahead.
To sum up what I have been saying I should like to quote something I read lately. It is as follows:
Consider this: Alone, among the major nations, your country has shown government surpluses for
2592	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Johnston the last seven years. Your national debt has been reduced substantially since 1946, and now stands at one of the lowest per capita rates of any country on earth. Your national income leaped ahead by $1 billion last year to make it the highest in history. Your gross national product increased 7 per cent to a record high of $23 billion, and wages and salaries advanced 12 per cent. And now, for 1953, your government has reduced your income taxes, your corporation and other taxes, and yet has budgeted for a record revenue and yet another surplus.
I recall the whispers of death of 1930 to 1935. Sometimes I do not like to hear those criticisms because I do not believe some of these people believe them to be so. In a young country such as ours, just starting on a major expansion, let us be inspired by these words of Lord Tennyson:
We sailed wherever ships could sail,
We founded many a mighty state,
Pray God our greatness may not fail Through craven fears of being great!
Indeed Canada is the champion country of the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduced his budget it was hailed with great acclaim by all the newspapers, particularly those which support the Liberal party. It probably was intended to be that way because the government no doubt intends this to be the very last budget before the coming election. One of my friends says "the last budget-stop".	It
probably will be.
The government is making every effort to see that they win the confidence of the people by this budget, but I am afraid they are going to be doomed to disappointment.
Yet it is a sad thing, Mr. Speaker, when we have a political party in this country that takes advantages of a coming election to try to deceive the public. Whether it is intentional or unintentional, the results could well be the same.
When the minister was introducing his budget he stated that the income tax reduction for the full year would be 11 per cent. Well, technically that may be correct; but as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, this budget- and the minister knew it quite well-will not extend over a full year. It will be divided on the 1st of July and for the following six months the reduction will be 11 per cent. It will not be for the whole fiscal year; it could not possibly be. Every year we have a new budget introduced, and every time there is a budget there is a tax change. Now, Mr. Speaker, I say that is deliberate deceit and it cannot be classed as anything else-trickery and foolery, in an endeavour to deceive the voting public.


Mr. Speaker, more taxes will be taken from the people of Canada this year than ever before. According to the budgetary estimate the figure is $4,473 million and, when you add the old age security tax which everyone must pay amounting to $280 million, it makes the colossal sum of $4,753 million. That is the largest budget in the history of Canada.
So next year the people face this problem of having to dig down in their pockets and shell out more taxes under this Liberal administration than have ever been taken in any single year from the people of Canada in all its history. Definitely there was a reduction in taxation of 5J per cent, and that reduction was spread over a great number of items, very trivial in some cases but still it was spread over them, giving a false impression to the people of Canada that they were receiving a great tax reduction. As a matter of fact our total tax reduction this year does not amount to any more than the surplus the government had last year.
In the first nine months of last year there was a surplus of $721 million and then, when the Minister of Finance had spent everything that he could spend, he still had $250 million left over that he did not know what to do with, so he applied it to the national debt. When we talk about the great splash in tax reduction it does no more than equal the excess taxation of last year. So we must realize that there are going to be more taxes, and not less.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) in speaking the other day pointed out that he had done some calculating in this regard, and had calculated that the per capita tax this coming year would be $340 for every man, woman and child in Canada. For a family of five it would be $1,700. That is the average tax per family and I am telling you, Mr. Speaker, that it is more than the average earnings of the greatest percentage of people in this country. It is estimated that 75 per cent of the people of Canada earn less than $3,000 per year. Therefore it will take the average family a whole year to pay that amount of tax.
When we talk of the great reduction that was made in these taxes it pays us to have a look at the tables and just see whether the people of Canada are receiving such a great reduction in taxation, particularly when we have to remind ourselves that Canada is more prosperous now than it has ever been. The minister has said on many occasions that the only possible way you can reduce taxes is by working longer hours, working harder and producing more. Last year we achieved a record. We produced more than we had ever produced in the history of this

country; and yet we had a tax reduction this year only equal to the surplus of last year.
At page 2125 of Hansard for February 19 we have the tax tables, and on an income of $1,500 a single taxpayer will have a tax reduction of the magnificent amount of $3. On $2,000 he will have saved $5. On $2,500 he will have saved $9; and on $3,000 he will have saved the magnificent sum of $12.

speechtext:
If you are lucky enough, and maybe my hon. friend is in this group, to have earned $400,000 then you would have saved $26,811. Then some of my friends across the way try to tell us that this is not a rich man's budget. It is going to be a pretty difficult thing to prove to the people of Canada that they have had very much in the way of relief in this budget.
According to the tables a married man earning $2,500 will have a reduction of $3. If he earns $3,000-and remember that 75 per cent of the people of Canada earn $3,000 or less-a married man with no dependents will save exactly $5. That is a magnificent saving. If you were a married man in the $400,000 class, without dependents, you would save $26,736. Do you know that the saving on that one individual's taxes amounts to more than the entire earnings of eight ordinary families? It pays to be in the rich brackets if you want to get some relief from this government.
It is true, and I would not want to try to deny it for a moment, that the reduction was spread over quite a few articles, and that is a big boasting point of those on the government side of the house when they try to fool the public into believing that great tax relief was given to everyone. For instance, there is the stamp tax. One of the members of the Social Credit party was pointing out the other day that it has taken the minister ten or fifteen years to come to the conclusion that this stamp tax was a nuisance tax. So, just before the election, lo and behold he decides that he should drop the nuisance tax. Now, I ask you how many people are going to receive any benefit from the removal of the stamp tax. I am probably an average wage earner in the country, Mr. Speaker, but I venture to say that I do not write a dozen cheques in a whole year, because I have not that kind of money. If I were like some of my hon. friends across the aisle, who figure their income tax in three, four, five and six figures, then I might write a lot of cheques; but I think I am quite safe in saying that 75 per cent of the people in Canada never write a dozen cheques in a whole year. What good is the repeal of the stamp tax C8108-1651
The Budget-Mr. Johnston going to do them? True, it is a nuisance tax and it should have been taken off long ago.
Then the farmers got some assistance. Yes, sir, they got the excise tax removed from plow bolts. That was quite a concession; and there are a few similar items. But plows in western Canada are becoming obsolete. They are not being used to a great extent any more. More modern machinery is taking their place, for instance the one-way disc. So they take the excise duty off plow bolts. Well, that is all there is to help agriculture. Again that is an effort to give a false impression that the farmers of the country are getting some tax relief.
The radio licences have been abolished. For some years now we in this party have contended that the radio licence fee was another tax that could be classed as a nuisance tax. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) it cost us over $700,000 to collect. The cost of collecting was out of all proportion to the benefits received. Now the minister, just before an election, decides to remove this radio licence fee. It could have been removed just as easily a year ago, and we would probably have saved this country a lot of money. It is not such a benevolent thing to have removed the radio licence fee because the government knows, just as well as every member in this house, that just as fast as television comes in, just so fast is radio going to go out. It is only going to be a matter of a few years until radio licences would not be sold anyway because the people would not be buying radios. I do not mean to say, Mr. Speaker, that we will not be paying for the operations of the C.B.C. The revenue from this licence fee used to be turned over to the C.B.C., but now they are going to receive the 15 per cent excise tax on television and radio sets.
It is true that there is going to be no television licence fee, but there is going to be a great deal more revenue brought in by the 15 per cent excise tax than there was before. Now no one will be permitted to bring television sets from the United States under the $100 exemption. What does that mean? It means that we are creating a monopoly in this country for television. Most of these television sets are going to be shipped in from the United States, in exactly the same way that radios were. Over in the United States you can buy a television set for half the price you pay in Canada. Had the minister decided to reduce the customs duty on television sets, there would have been some sense to that. I say that advisedly, Mr. Speaker, because the minister did reduce the tax on cigarettes by 4 cents a package or $2 a thousand, and at the same time he reduced the tax he did reduce the customs duty.

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
What was the result of that? The people of Canada who smoke cigarettes received some material benefits because not only was the amount of the tax cut removed from the price of the cigarettes, but the companies themselves lowered the price. I have always maintained, Mr. Speaker, and I still say, that one of the best ways for the government to control prices in this country, or to bring prices down, is not necessarily the lowering of the tax rate only, but they should also lower the tariff. In the case of cigarettes that is exactly what happened. When the excise tax was reduced on cigarettes a year ago, the tobacco companies were hollering to blue heaven that they were not making enough profit. The minute the customs tariff was reduced, the companies brought down the price of their cigarettes.
Had that been done for television sets there would have been some sense to it. Now the people have to pay a 15 per cent excise tax and also the 10 per cent sales tax, and in addition to that the people of Canada are going to be paying twice the amount for television sets that the people of the United States have to pay. We cannot even bring them in from the United States under the $100 exemption.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I should mention that 1 per cent reduction in the medical expense allowance. It seems to me that when a government is endeavouring to bring down a budget it should take into consideration very seriously those people who are most affected. I cannot think of any class that could be relieved more than those people who are continually suffering from illness, particularly those in the low income brackets. I repeat that 75 per cent of the people in Canada are earning less than $3,000 a year. I believe the Minister of Finance should have found it possible to completely eliminate that 4 per cent floor on medical expenses. It would not have meant a great loss of revenue to the government, but it would have meant a great deal to those people who are so hard pressed.
I do not think it should make much difference who makes a suggestion. In this case it was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). If the suggestion is a good one, a good government should take advantage of it. The only relief we got in this case was a reduction of 1 per cent.
Some of the members on the opposite side have taken objection to this being called a rich man's budget. The other day when the leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), was speaking he put on the record some figures in relation to corporations. At the outset I want to say that I, like the leader of this party,


believe that our corporations should be in a good, sound financial position. I think they have been. The prosperity within Canada indicates that our corporations are in a sound position. When speaking on Tuesday, February 24, the leader of this party pointed out that in the ten-year period between 1940 and 1950 the accumulated undistributed profits were $4,952 million, after paying costs as well as dividends of $4,276 million, and also after setting aside depreciation of $6,338 million. That is certainly evidence that our industries, large and small, have been doing fairly well. In fact, the hon. member went on to point out that in the two years 1951 and 1952 it is estimated that corporation profits were greater than in the ten-year period, which would mean over $6 billion. Therefore I do not think our big industries are too badly off.
Then we heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) refer to the sugar industry and say that they have made sufficient profits so they could well afford to pay the beet growers a little more for the work they were doing. He certainly indicated that the sugar industry of this country was in a sound, healthy position, and that it was making such large profits that it could well afford to pay the beet growers a little bit more. The other night the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair), when speaking to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), pointed out that some of our small industries had done extremely well and had been able to expand their capital investment quite substantially.
When we have statements like those coming from two responsible ministers-one of the senior ministers of the government and one who I have no hesitation in saying is the best and most capable minister in the government-nobody in this house will dare to say that we had to give greater concessions to industry at the expense of these people in the lower income brackets. I am quite sure there is no member on the government side of the house who would contradict what has been said by these two ministers.
Let me say just a word about the national debt. Some of the government members have gone to a great deal of pains to say what has been done in regard to the national debt. This complete story was put on the record by other members of this party, but I just want to review it for a moment. In the table which was put on Hansard by the minister, he referred to the net debt. It seems to me that when speaking of debt it is much sounder to refer to the funded debt, which at the end of March 31 was $14,837,630,000. The interest

charge alone on that debt was $409,456,495. The odd thing about this matter, Mr. Speaker, is that when the government are saying what they have done for this country by reducing the national debt and how much they have reduced the interest rates, thereby saving the people a great amount of interest each year, it is well to remember also that it was this party who built up that debt.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was the Liberal party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not say it was the Social Credit party that built up this debt. Of course it was the Liberal party. Any intelligent Liberal would know that because in the province of Alberta the government have got rid of their debt, or nearly so.
But let us look at the table which the Minister of Finance put on Hansard at page 2122. In 1939, according to him, our net debt stood at $3,153 million. By 1946 this Liberal government has raised that debt to $13,421 million. That was all under a Liberal administration. In 1952 they had reduced it some, down to $11,185 million. But between 1939 and 1952 this Liberal government had increased our debt by over $8 billion. Then they say, "Well, we have reduced your total debt. Haven't we done wonders?"

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And a surplus every year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And a surplus every year which was obtained by overtaxation. Then the minister goes on in the same table and points out that our per capita debt in 1939 was $280, and that at the end of 1952 that per capita debt stood at $775. Then they say, "See what we have done." The interest charges alone on that debt are almost twice as much as the tax reductions this year.
Hon. members in this house will recall that when the Social Credit government went into power in Alberta in 1935 they had to pay 51 cents out of every dollar of tax money for interest on the debt. They have now reduced that debt down to a point where they pay only 5 cents out of their tax dollar; and that 5 cents pays not only the interest but will reduce the entire capital debt in a matter of a few years. If this government wanted to do something, and if they really wanted to do away with the national debt, they would take their pattern from the government of the province of Alberta. They could not get better teachers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Find some oil.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no oil in Ottawa.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They do a lot of greasing of the wheels, though.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everything is too well oiled here.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For a few minutes I want to speak about agriculture in relation to the farmers' problems. I was greatly interested the other day when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was telling us how prosperous Canada was. This is a prosperous country. Everyone will agree with that statement. But that prosperity has been the result of the efforts of the provinces, not of the federal government. If you like, we can take the province of Alberta as an example. Everybody is using it as an example of thrift and good management. We find that in 1935 the province of Alberta could not even begin to sell a bond issue. Their credit was nil. Now of course its credit rating is one of the highest. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce was talking about the prosperity of Canada, and he gave us a good account of his trip to Latin America. He was telling us how prospects there were for building up trade. I think the minister did a wise thing when he made that trip to Latin America because, as the evidence proves, our trade relations with Latin America in the last year were falling down badly under the administration of this Liberal government. So just before an election he takes a trip to Latin America and comes back here and says, "Everything is fine now. I have just been over there and maybe next year or the year after we shall begin to pick up some of our lost trade."
The other day I was reading an article in the Ottawa Citizen of February 28. It was headed "Reduction in Total Value of Exports" and reads in part as follows:
Canada's exports to Latin America dropped by more than $10 million during January, with the biggest cuts showing in shipments to Brazil and Mexico.
In a report on Canada's exports to all countries during the month, the bureau of statistics yesterday estimated shipments to Latin America slipped to $18,225,000 from $28,764,000 in January 1952.
With export volume up 3 per cent but prices down 5 per cent from a year ago, value of Canada's total shipments during January eased to $321,300,000 from $328,500,500. The monthly report on imports likely will be published in about a week.
The slackening in prices, if it continues, will make it tough for Canada to repeat last year's record exports of $4,400 million.
It is therefore high time the Minister of Trade and Commerce went over to Latin America to see whether he could not bolster up the already crumbling walls of trade.
Mr. Speaker, wherever you look there is evidence that our agricultural industry is heading for bad times. I do not say that in

The Budget-Mr. Johnston order to be a pessimist. I think the thing can be remedied if the government takes the advice that it is given on occasion. In the Ottawa Journal of February 17, 1953 there appeared an article headed "Sees Some Signs Agriculture Prosperity Has Passed Peak" and which reads in part as follows:
There was "some evidence" that the peak of prosperity for agriculture as a whole was passed, L. W. Pearsall, director of the federal Department of Agriculture's marketing service told delegates to the 31st annual meeting of the Canadian horticultural council Monday.
He noted that in recent years there had been a decline in both gross and net farm income and there was ahead the prospect of lower prices for a variety of commodities.
That was the opinion of the director of the federal Department of Agriculture marketing service. He should know something about agricultural prices and prosperity, and his prediction is that the prosperity of agriculture is fast dropping. Then in the Calgary Albertan of December 24, 1952, under the heading "Farmers' Cash Income Shows 9-Month Decrease" we find this:
Ottawa (CP)-Cash income received by Canadian farmers totalled $1,840 million in the first nine months of 1952, the bureau of statistics reported.
This is a decline of more than $35 million from $1,876 million in the same period last year, the bureau said.
The cash comes from the sale of farm products and from payments made by the Canadian wheat board under western grain pool marketing arrangements.
There we have been shown that agriculture has lost $35 million in nine months. That is not a good sign for this country. There has been a 19 per cent drop in agricultural wholesale prices while at the same time there has been a 7 per cent increase in the production costs of the farm. That was given by the bureau of statistics, so I guess it must be right.
A moment ago, while I was speaking, somebody mentioned oil. He said, "What about the oil in Alberta?" May I say that oil production in Alberta has been growing tremendously and that the government has obtained a good deal of money from it. In fact the prospects are that oil will be found in other parts of Canada as well. But the oil production in 1951 was only $120 million. When you compare that with the figure for agricultural production, it will be seen that oil is so far behind that it never will catch up to agriculture. So the thing we must be watching carefully is that we keep agriculture in a sound and healthy position. Unless the policy of this government is changed in such a way that we will be able to recover some of our lost markets, agriculture is heading for a bad time.


We have the wheat board, a most commendable institution, and I would not want to see it dispensed with. I do believe, however, that prices should be higher. I believe the wheat board should be allowed to sell grain at the highest possible price. If the federal government wishes to give wheat to Great Britain or to any other country, then it should buy the wheat from the wheat board at the current price, reserving the right to dispose of it at any price it wishes.
The international wheat agreement is going to be a most important feature in agriculture, but I believe it would be unwise to say at this time what the price should be, at a time when negotiations are taking place. However, those engaged in agriculture across this country are determined that the floor should be raised, as well as the ceiling. Agriculture must have a greater return for the things it produces, particularly when one realizes that those things the farmer has to buy have continually increased in price.
If, by chance, agriculture is ignored, as it has been in this budget, and there is no concerted effort to bring prosperity to the farm, then the farming element in this country will be forced to take the matter into their own hands and adjust production in such a way as to maintain prices. Other industries do that, and agriculture may be forced to do it. I do not suggest that is a proper solution, but it may have to be adopted.
I was interested the other day in reading an article from the Rural Co-operator of Tuesday, January 13, 1953, which states:
A trend toward approval of a policy of planned production has been apparent among farm people for some time. Last week the Ontario federation of agriculture annual meeting, representing some 80,000 Ontario farmers, gave approval to such a policy. They asked the government to supply reliable statistics to enable farmers to plan production of only enough food to supply the home market in order to avoid overproduction and market collapse.
Such planning, perhaps overdue at this time, appears to be the only course open at present to farm people if they are to avoid disaster. Farmers cannot go on producing for a world market if governments cannot solve the monetary difficulties that prevent distribution of food to the areas where it is needed.
Canadians, in general, may be shocked to hear farmers talking about planned production and farm people themselves have been hesitant about adopting such a program but it appears obvious that overproduction and low prices would ultimately limit food production more drastically than the contemplated program for intelligent planning.
That in itself should be sufficient warning to this government to do something about agriculture.
I had intended to say something about housing, but I shall not develop that subject

tonight because of lack of time. I would wish to save the discussion until a time when, having started it, I can finish it. I believe that opportunity will present itself when we have before us the estimates of the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters).
I should also like to have spoken on coal and the setting up of a national fuel policy for Canada, but time won't permit me to do that.
When referring to the minister under whom this matter comes, however, there is one point I would like to mention. On this occasion I thank him publicly for the very great consideration and co-operation he has shown to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and myself in regard to the problems we have been facing in Banff national park. We have been endeavouring to open a trout farm at that point. It will be a worth-while asset to the people of Banff and to the tourist business. The minister has been most co-operative in this matter. Then in the last few months other difficulties have arisen in the Banff area, and we have found the minister most considerate. Some of these things have been in the form of nuisances that have caused grief to the people concerned.
For instance, the superintendent of the park recently brought down a regulation under which he charged a licence fee of $5 for each cat. I have never heard of cats being licensed before, and certainly never to the extent of soaking everyone $5 for each cat. This is a sample of the things that have been disturbing the people in that area, and I wish to say again that the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) has been exceedingly co-operative in every respect. Banff is a national tourist centre. According to the public account, we spent last year $1,503,197 in advertising to attract tourists to Canada. The tourist business is big business, aggregating last year somewhere around $300 million.
Earlier this evening in the railway committee room we saw a most interesting moving picture depicting some of the value of the tourist business to this country, and we should be encouraging that business. But if we are going to encourage it, then we must make every effort to see to it that our tourist resorts, of which Banff is one of the most outstanding, are developed so that they can accommodate the tourists who come. As I have pointed out, we are spending large sums of money to advertise our national parks. Last year we spent over $30,437 for road maps alone, and $185,359 for a publication called "Vacations Unlimited". Those are just two of the many items set forth in the public accounts.
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery
We are spending millions of dollars to advertise our tourist attractions, and for that reason we should make our tourist resorts among the finest in the world. Banff is an outstanding example of one to which particular attention should be directed. We should make every effort to see that tourists who come to Canada do not leave without first having visited the great Banff national park in the province of Alberta.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this budget debate may I say that this is the first one to which I have had the opportunity of listening. I listened with keen interest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and, while I speak only for myself, I am sure other hon. members will agree that one must admire the minister in that he is a good-natured, genial and able speaker. He presented a convincing argument, one that captivated those who listened to him.
I could not help thinking, however, that the personality and the magnetism of the minister far exceeded the statement he was presenting. The budget itself is deserving of a lot of thought and study. I can see some sunshine in it; but, Mr. Speaker, I can also see some gloom.
Coming as I do from an agricultural constituency, I am going to devote most of my time to discussing the problems of a group who, I believe, should receive more consideration. The budget debate gives me an opportunity to voice some of the complaints of this forgotten group, the farmers; those citizens who toil long hours and under great handicaps to produce food, the most vital necessity of civilization. I do not hesitate to speak for farmers generally, because what I intend to say will apply more or less to farmers as a whole across this country.
Where will you find a group in Canada who work longer hours? Where would you find a group where the wives and children are obliged to get out in the fields to assist the heads of the families in order that the products of their labour may be harvested and marketed? Where is there a group that receives such a small net return? I notice that usually when the government gives any figures it indicates gross returns. To me such figures do not give a true picture of the farmer's position.
I do not need to labour the point in order to make out a case for these neglected people. I am not speaking simply to criticize. I think all I have to do is refer the government to the farmers themselves, and their situation will speak for them. The farmer's net income is declining. This group of people have contributed chiefly to the lowered cost
2598	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Montgomery of living, as is shown by the recent index. That decrease in the index was brought about mainly by lower food prices. If this government is going to take credit for the general growth and prosperity of this country, it must also accept responsibility for the plight of these primary producers.
Instead of placing agriculture at the top or at least giving it high priority in national planning, it would appear from all reports that it is being neglected. In New Brunswick agriculture ranks first as an industry providing livelihood for our people. More than 27,000 people are engaged in agriculture or are dependent upon it, which is approximately 10,000 more than the number depending upon any other single industry. The production of food is important, not only for our own people but for other nations. I do not believe there can be overproduction of food as long as there are hungry people in the world.
It seems to me that our farming industry and the means of distribution of food should be given top priority in national and international planning. Why are so many of our young men leaving their farms to take employment in other industry? Many do not even sell their farms; they just dispose of their stock and equipment and walk off. Why have the sales of farms dropped in the last two years? Why are there so many idle farms? There are a great many idle farms in my province. Invariably these people who are leaving give three reasons: the high cost of equipment needed to run a farm, high taxes, and the low prices received for the products they have to sell.
Even though they work long hours they do not make as good a living or enjoy the same privileges as labour employed in other industries. I was glad to hear the minister state that the 15 per cent excise tax will not apply to tires and tubes purchased by farmers for their machinery. His interpretation was certainly necessary, as some of those who are administering the act felt that it did apply.
I am grateful that this point has been cleaned up and the farmers will not be obliged to pay that tax.
The benefits received by farmers through the abolition of the radio licence, stamps on cheques and the reduction in the income tax are not going to permit them to sell more products or increase their standard of living. In other words these reductions are not going

The Budget-Mr. Montgomery argument that the freight rate structure between the Atlantic provinces and central Canada must be based on the necessity of permitting the products of the provinces by the sea to be landed in central Canada so they may be placed in that market on a competitive basis with the same types of products grown and produced in the central Canadian area. Otherwise freight rates and other charges can be barriers which isolate the maritimes from the rest of Canada and result in nullifying the whole idea of allowing us in
the east to enjoy the fruits of economic union as was the dream of the founders of this country.
On motion of Mr. Montgomery the debate was adjourned.
